glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Hannah asks the LORD for a son, and God answers by raising Samuel—a faithful servant and prophet who will prepare Israel for a king.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: At Shiloh, during the days of Eli the priest, Hannah carries the sorrow of childlessness and her rival’s relentless provocation.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:

  • 1 Samuel 1:9–18 — Hannah’s Prayer and Vow at Shiloh

  • 1 Samuel 1:19–23 — The LORD Remembers Hannah, and Samuel Is Born

  • 1 Samuel 1:24–28 — Samuel Lent to the LORD

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition which I asked of Him.” (1 Samuel 1:27, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Hannah comes to Shiloh with a longing no one around her can satisfy. Peninnah provokes her, Elkanah loves her, and Eli initially misunderstands her. But Hannah brings her sorrow to the LORD. She pours out her soul, asks for a son, and vows that the child will belong to Him all his life.

Hannah comes before the LORD, pours out her troubles, and asks Him for a son. As she prays, God reveals His desire to raise up someone who will serve Him. Hannah responds by partnering with God's purpose, promising that if He gives her a son, she will give him back to the LORD for his entire life. God answers her prayer, and Hannah fulfills her promise.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Samuel 1:1–8 — Elkanah’s Household and Hannah’s Grief

Elkanah goes up yearly to worship at Shiloh, while Hannah, though loved, grieves over her childlessness and Peninnah’s repeated provocation. Her husband’s love cannot take away that grief.

1 Samuel 1:9–18 — Hannah’s Prayer and Vow at Shiloh

At Shiloh, Hannah pours out her soul to the LORD and vows to dedicate a son to Him for life. Eli first mistakes her for drunk, then blesses her petition, and she leaves with her face no longer sad.

1 Samuel 1:19–23 — The LORD Remembers Hannah, and Samuel Is Born

The LORD remembers Hannah, and she bears Samuel. She stays home until he is weaned, and Elkanah agrees with her plan, asking the LORD to establish His word.

1 Samuel 1:24–28 — Samuel Lent to the LORD

Hannah brings Samuel with offerings to Shiloh and tells Eli that the LORD has granted her petition. She gives the child to the LORD for as long as he lives, and the family worships there.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hannah brings her deepest desire to the LORD, and He remembers her and answers her request. She receives Samuel with gratitude and gives him back in worship.

God’s answer reaches beyond Hannah’s household. He raises a prophet to speak His word, restores faithful service before Him, and prepares the way for Israel’s kings. A personal prayer becomes part of God’s purpose for a nation.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Prayer from the heart. Hannah brings her anguish and desire openly before the LORD (vv. 10–16).

The LORD answers. God remembers Hannah and gives her the son she requested (vv. 19–20, 27).

A life given to God. Hannah dedicates Samuel to the LORD before he is born and fulfills her vow afterward (vv. 11, 24–28).

God’s preparation of faithful leadership. Samuel’s birth begins the raising of a servant who will minister before God and lead Israel (vv. 20, 27–28).

Worship through the whole journey. Hannah comes to Shiloh in sorrow and returns with Samuel in thanksgiving and surrender (vv. 7, 10, 24–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Shiloh. Israel’s central place of worship in this period, where the tabernacle stood and Eli served as priest.

Vow. A solemn promise to God. Hannah pledges to give her son to the LORD for his entire life (v. 11).

“Poured out my soul.” Hannah’s description of bringing her deep grief and longing before God in prayer (v. 15).

“No razor shall come upon his head.” A sign associated with the Nazirite vow of being set apart for God, expressing Samuel’s lifelong dedication to Him (v. 11; Numbers 6:5).

“The LORD remembered her.” The LORD turns toward Hannah in mercy and answers her prayer (v. 19).

Samuel / “lent to the LORD.” Hannah connects Samuel’s name with asking the LORD for him. She now gives him to God for life (vv. 20, 27–28).

culture.title: We are a House of Prayer
culture.statement: Jesus identified His Father’s house as a House of Prayer. We assemble to seek the heart of the Father and partner with Him in faith, inquiry, intercession, supplication, petition, lament, and thanksgiving. We contend for mercy, righteousness, healing, and justice, believing that God transforms lives, cities, and nations through a praying Church.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 1
culture.html:
Hannah brings her deepest sorrow directly before the Lord. At Shiloh, “she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed to the LORD and wept in anguish” (1 Samuel 1:10). Her prayer includes lament, petition, surrender, and ultimately thanksgiving and worship. She does not hide her anguish or allow it to drive her away from God. She pours out her soul before Him. Even before Samuel is conceived, something changes in Hannah: after praying and receiving Eli’s blessing, “her face was no longer sad” (1 Samuel 1:18). Prayer has brought her burden into the presence and care of God before the answer has appeared.

This gives real substance to being a House of Prayer. Prayer is not merely something the church schedules. It is the life of a people who bring their need, grief, desire, and future before the Lord because they believe He hears. Hannah’s prayer also reaches beyond personal relief. The son she asks for is given back to God for His purposes. God answers one woman’s anguished prayer in a way that will eventually affect an entire nation. A praying church learns to bring everything before God while remaining open to the larger purposes He may accomplish through the answer.

culture.title: Vision
culture.statement: East Gate exists to teach you how to hear God’s voice, connect with Him daily and walk with Him in obedience.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 1
culture.html:
Hear. Connect. Obey. Hannah heard God as she prayed, connected with His heart and purpose for the son He would give her, and obeyed by giving Samuel wholly back to Him. Her obedience reached far beyond her own life. The child she surrendered became the prophet through whom God spoke to Israel and anointed David as king. One woman heard God, came into agreement with His heart, and obeyed, and through her obedience God helped change the course of a nation.

At East Gate, that is not a one-time moment; it is a rhythm we return to daily, the way Hannah’s answer did not arrive the day she prayed. It looks like keeping a daily Secret Place where we actually listen, not just bring requests. It looks like testing what we sense against Scripture and the people who know us well, the way both Elkanah and Eli had a part in confirming what Hannah had heard. And it looks like obeying even when it costs us something over years, not only when it is easy. Hannah’s obedience did not end when Samuel was born; it carried through the nursing years, the weaning, and the morning she walked him to Shiloh and left him there. Walking with God often looks the same in that it requires a long obedience and not just a single response.

culture.title: HONOR || Through His Eyes
culture.statement: Relationships are protected when we ascribe heaven’s value to the people around us. Like Jesus, we choose to interact with people, not as they deserve, but according to their God-given value.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 1
culture.html: Being wrongly judged does not give us permission to dishonor someone else. Hannah answered Eli firmly but respectfully (1:15–16). She could have exposed the failures in his own household or answered his accusation with contempt. Instead, she told him the truth without dishonoring him. Our response to someone else’s failure says as much about our own heart as it does about theirs.

culture.title: Communication
culture.statement: We “real talk” because we desire real relationships built on trust. We have 100% of our conversations, choosing to be authentic, honest, and open with one another. Awkward today, stronger tomorrow.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 1
culture.html: Hannah had every reason to stay quiet, or to answer Eli with an edge. He had just accused her, in the middle of her grief, of being drunk. Instead she told him the plain truth — “I have not been drinking... I was pouring out my soul before the LORD” — clearly, but without contempt (1:15–16). That is what real talk looks like when it is done well. Honest communication does not have to come out sharp, and grace does not require us to stay silent. At East Gate, when someone in leadership misjudges us or gets the wrong idea about our heart, we choose to handle it maturely, having 100% of the conversation with that person. We do not stay silent and let it fester in our heart. We do not complain to someone else. We communicate, plainly, and humbly the way Hannah did with a man who held real authority over her. Awkward conversations handled with humility instead of silence or sharpness are what actually build trust. That is what makes us stronger tomorrow.

culture.title: We Empower Women
culture.statement: We actively endorse and promote godly women in ministry, creating opportunities for them to step into their God-given calling. We empower women to fulfill the biblical purpose and destiny God has placed on their lives, equipping them to lead, serve, and advance His kingdom.
culture.label: Living It in 1 Samuel 1
culture.html:
Hannah stands at the center of this chapter’s movement. She seeks God, pours out her soul before Him, hears God’s heart, makes a solemn vow, receives His answer by faith, bears Samuel, and faithfully presents him to the Lord. The future Samuel is not introduced first through a king, priest, or national leader, but through the prayer, faith, and obedience of a woman who takes God seriously. Her husband recognizes the importance of what she has heard from the Lord as he tells her, “Do what seems best to you” (1 Samuel 1:23). When the time comes, Hannah herself brings Samuel to the house of the Lord and testifies concerning the child for whom she prayed.

That gives biblical substance to a culture that makes room for godly women to follow the calling God places on their lives. At East Gate, that means watching for the Hannahs among us — women marked by depth in prayer, discernment, and obedience — and inviting them into real ministry, not just supporting roles behind the scenes: teaching, leading intercession, shepherding, and carrying spiritual authority as God has gifted them. It also asks something of the Elkanahs among us. When a woman senses God calling her to something costly, the leader who says, “Do what seems best to you,” and actually makes room for it, is living this out too. Empowering women recognizes that God works through women whose faith, prayer, obedience, and ability to hear His voice, become instruments of His purposes.

items.title: The Trap of Misdirected Compensation (1 Samuel 1:4–8)
items.html: Elkanah tried to fix Hannah’s grief with a double portion of meat and sweet words: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” It is a classic picture of human beings trying to heal a spiritual void with material or emotional compensation. He meant well, and he loved her, but the remedy did not fit the wound. Year after year the portions were handed out at Shiloh, and year after year Hannah still wept and would not eat. This section warns us not to settle for the “double portion” of natural comfort while our soul is aching for the fulfillment of God’s promise. Hannah would not let Elkanah’s love become an anesthetic to her prophetic burden. Many believers have been quietly sedated by good things: a comfortable home, kind words, a full table. These are gifts, but when they are used to numb a longing God Himself has stirred, they become a trap.
items.q: Elkanah tried to fix Hannah’s grief with a double portion of meat and sweet words: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

items.title: The Barrenness of the Flesh and the Groaning for the Spirit (1 Samuel 1:1–8)
items.html: This section establishes the absolute bankruptcy of natural solutions to spiritual problems. A respected Ephraimite family, a faithful yearly pilgrimage, generous portions, a loving husband, a houseful of children by another wife: none of it could produce what only God could give. Every natural resource in Elkanah’s home was spent, and Hannah was still barren. That is exactly where God wanted the story to stand before the next scene opens. The flesh can furnish a household, but it cannot fill a womb that God has closed. Only when every natural remedy has failed does the soul begin to groan for the Spirit.
items.q: This section establishes the absolute bankruptcy of natural solutions to spiritual problems.

items.title: The Divine Strategy of Orchestrated Lack (1 Samuel 1:2–8)
items.html: Viewed as a whole, this section reveals that God will often engineer a crisis in the natural realm to secure a victory in the spiritual realm. If Hannah had conceived as easily as Peninnah, she might have been content raising ordinary sons in the hill country of Ephraim. Israel would have had another farmer; it would not have had a prophet. God starved Hannah of normalcy so that she would demand a miracle. The LORD had closed her womb, the rival provoked her because of it, and her husband could not comfort her out of it, and every one of those pressures pushed her toward the altar. Her barrenness was not a punishment, but a divine staging ground. What looks like God withholding may be God preparing us to ask for something far greater than we would ever have asked for in comfort.
items.q: Viewed as a whole, this section reveals that God will often engineer a crisis in the natural realm to secure a victory in the spiritual realm.

items.title: The Two Distractions: The Rival and the Comforter (1 Samuel 1:6–8)
items.html: The interplay between Hannah, Peninnah, and Elkanah reveals two distractions every seeker of God faces: the provocation of the enemy and the pacification of the flesh. Peninnah tried to destroy Hannah through cruelty; Elkanah tried to soothe her into comfortable complacency: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” One pressed her toward despair, the other toward settling. Both, in different ways, would have kept her from the altar. The rival says, “You will never have it.” The comforter says, “You do not really need it.” The true spiritual seeker must reject both the despair offered by the rival and the spiritual mediocrity offered by well-meaning loved ones. Hannah refused both voices, and rose to pray.
items.q: The interplay between Hannah, Peninnah, and Elkanah reveals two distractions every seeker of God faces: the provocation of the enemy and the pacification of the flesh.

items.title: The Spiritual Geography of Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3, 7)
items.html: It matters that this agony peaked “year by year” at Shiloh. Shiloh was where the ark of the covenant rested before it was captured; it was the place of God’s presence in Israel. Hannah’s grief was magnified precisely because she was near the presence of God. The closer one gets to the authentic presence of God, the more intolerable one’s spiritual barrenness becomes.
items.q: It matters that this agony peaked “year by year” at Shiloh.

sections.title: Hannah’s Prayer and Vow at Shiloh

items.title: The Hinge of History Turning on a Woman’s Tears (1 Samuel 1:9–18)
items.html: This section captures the moment the era of the Judges begins to end and the era of the prophets and kings begins to dawn. The bridge between those eras is not built with a sword, a council, or a military campaign. It is built on the weeping of a desperate woman at the tabernacle. No elders gathered, no general rallied the tribes, no priest sought the LORD for the nation. One barren woman rose from a table, wept before the LORD, and made a vow, and the prophet who would anoint Israel’s first two kings was conceived in that prayer. The spiritual weight of this section is staggering: God shifts the destiny of a nation because one woman refuses to remain unfruitful. Never underestimate what God may hang on the hinge of one person’s prayer.
items.q: This section captures the moment the era of the Judges begins to end and the era of the prophets and kings begins to dawn.

items.title: The Old Wineskin and the New Wine (1 Samuel 1:9–16)
items.html: The exchange between Eli and Hannah depicts the passing of a torch. Eli represents the old religious establishment: seated, later physically blind (3:2), spiritually dull, relying on outward appearances, and assuming that passionate spiritual expression must be intoxication. Hannah represents the new move of the Spirit: desperate, moving her lips in silent agony, about to bring forth a new prophetic order, filled not with wine but with the burden of God. When the church becomes institutionalized like Eli, it often persecutes the true intercessors like Hannah.
items.q: The exchange between Eli and Hannah depicts the passing of a torch.

items.title: The Exchange of Wills at the Altar (1 Samuel 1:10–18)
items.html: This section holds one of the most powerful transactions of the will in the Old Testament. Hannah came to the altar wanting a son for herself, to erase her shame. But in the fire of prayer, her will came into line with God’s. The vow, “I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life,” transformed her prayer from a petition for personal relief into a partnership for kingdom advancement. And in that place she heard from God; the vow was her agreement with His purpose, not a price paid to obtain a favor. God granted her request when her request came to serve His eternal purpose. The evidence followed quickly: she rose from the place of prayer with peace on her face before there was any child in her womb. This is a shadow of Christ in Gethsemane: “Not My will, but Yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The deepest prayers are not the ones in which we bend God to our desire, but the ones in which our desire is surrendered and returned to us, now carrying His purpose.
items.q: This section holds one of the most powerful transactions of the will in the Old Testament.

items.title: The Changing of the Guard at the Doorpost (1 Samuel 1:9–18)
items.html: Read together, these verses paint a dramatic transition of spiritual authority in Israel. Eli is heavy (4:18), seated, and spiritually blind, unable to tell the groaning of the Holy Spirit from the effects of alcohol. Hannah is fasting, weeping, moving, and spiritually attuned. The old system sits at the doorpost, while the new movement of God groans on the floor. And God bypasses the seated priest to partner with a weeping woman. Even Eli’s blessing, spoken without knowing what she asked, becomes a sign that the authority of the moment has already passed to the one who prayed. The old guard must make way for a new generation of desperate intercessors.
items.q: Read together, these verses paint a dramatic transition of spiritual authority in Israel.

items.title: The Blindness of the Seated Priest and the Sight of the Moving Woman (1 Samuel 1:9–18)
items.html: The juxtaposition of Eli and Hannah is a pointed critique of institutional religion emptied of the Spirit. Eli sits by the doorpost, static, managing the house, yet completely blind to the spiritual reality unfolding in front of him. He holds religious authority, yet he thinks the holiest woman in Israel is a drunkard. Meanwhile Hannah, who holds no office at all, has direct access to the throne room of heaven, and she becomes the mother of the prophet through whom God will speak to Israel. This illustrates how, in times of national spiritual decay, God frequently bypasses the “seated” religious professionals and entrusts His prophetic burdens to the marginalized, desperate people who are willing to pour out their souls. Familiarity with sacred things is not the same as spiritual discernment. We must never grow so used to the forms of worship that we fail to recognize a heart genuinely reaching for God, or so comfortable in our seat that God has to go around us.
items.q: The juxtaposition of Eli and Hannah is a pointed critique of institutional religion emptied of the Spirit.

items.title: The Romans 8 Intercession Model (1 Samuel 1:10–15)
items.html: This section is an Old Testament embodiment of Romans 8:26: the Spirit Himself makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered. Hannah has come to the end of her vocabulary. She prays in bitterness of soul; her lips move, but no sound comes out. She has gone beyond the reach of the intellect and is praying from the depths, pouring out her soul. When Eli demands an explanation, she has no polished prayer to quote, only an emptied heart. This teaches that the most powerful prayers are often the ones we cannot put into words. They are raw spiritual groanings, and the Father hears them and translates them perfectly. The person who says, “I don’t even know how to pray about this,” may be closer to Hannah’s prayer than the one with the most eloquent words.
items.q: This section is an Old Testament embodiment of Romans 8:26: the Spirit Himself makes intercession for us with groanings that cannot be uttered.

sections.title: The LORD Remembers Hannah, and Samuel Is Born

items.title: The Rhythm of Grace: From Petition to Presentation (1 Samuel 1:11–28)
items.html: The closing section reveals the complete life cycle of a God-breathed desire. It moves from petition (v. 11), to peace (v. 18), to conception and birth (vv. 19–20), to preparation and weaning (vv. 22–23), and finally to presentation (vv. 24–28). Each stage has its own test. Petition tests our honesty; peace tests our trust; birth tests our gratitude; weaning tests our patience; presentation tests our surrender. God does not give a blessing merely so we can hold it. He gives it so it can grow, mature, and eventually be returned to Him for His use. Many of us want to skip from petition straight to possession and stop there. Hannah’s story insists that the rhythm of grace is not complete until the gift is back in the hands of the Giver.
items.q: The closing section reveals the complete life cycle of a God-breathed desire.

items.title: The Pain of Keeping the Vow (1 Samuel 1:11, 21–28)
items.html: Reading this section requires us to feel the immense human cost of Hannah’s vow. The very thing she wept for, starved for, and agonized over for years is the very thing she now has to give away. She holds him only long enough to wean him, perhaps two to four years in that culture. It was one thing to promise her son to God while her womb was empty; it was another to give him back after she had nursed him and learned to love his face. Her desperation did not excuse her from keeping her word once the desperation ended. The depth of her spiritual maturity is astounding: her love for the LORD outstripped her love for the child she had so desperately wanted. An answer to prayer can test our hearts as severely as the waiting did. Do we love the Lord Himself, or only what we hoped He would give us?
items.q: Do we love the Lord Himself, or only what we hoped He would give us?

items.title: The Surrogate Mother of the Prophetic Order (1 Samuel 1:24–28)
items.html: Hannah acts as a steward, not an owner. By leaving her young son at the tabernacle, she points to the heart of God the Father, who gave His only Son to a dark, corrupt world for the sake of redemption. Shiloh was a wicked place under Hophni and Phinehas, yet Hannah placed her pure child into that polluted religious system, trusting God to keep him. She did not wait for Shiloh to be cleaned up before she gave God what He asked for; she gave, and trusted Him to protect what was His. The section then turns beautifully: “And he worshiped the LORD there.” The focus shifts from the mother to the child who will change the world. That is what true stewardship always does. It hands the story over, steps back, and lets what God birthed through us become His, not ours.
items.q: Hannah acts as a steward, not an owner.

items.title: The Principle of the Firstfruits (1 Samuel 1:24–28; 2:21)
items.html: Hannah practices the law of firstfruits in its fullest form. Samuel is the opener of her womb, the long-awaited prize. Yet instead of clutching him out of fear of returning to barrenness, she gives him away completely. She does not keep her first and best and offer God what comes later; she gives Him the first, before she knows if there will be any other. And by giving God her first and best, she unlocks the womb: 1 Samuel 2:21 reveals that she went on to bear three more sons and two daughters. Fear says, “If I give this up, I may never have anything again.” Faith says, “This was His before it was mine.” Surrendering our “Isaac” to God is the key to unlocking multiplication.
items.q: Hannah practices the law of firstfruits in its fullest form.

items.title: The Process of Spiritual Weaning (1 Samuel 1:22–24)
items.html: Hannah delayed the fulfillment of her vow until the child was weaned, which in ancient times could take up to three years. This introduces the spiritual principle of weaning. Before we can be released into our ultimate calling or temple service, we must be weaned off the milk of human comfort. A weaned child can digest solid food and survive apart from the mother. Ministry and destiny demand a season of hidden weaning before public release.
items.q: Hannah delayed the fulfillment of her vow until the child was weaned, which in ancient times could take up to three years.

items.title: The Theology of the Weaned Child (1 Samuel 1:22–28; Psalm 131:2)
items.html: In verse 22 Hannah refuses to go up to the house of the LORD until the child is weaned. Psalm 131 later uses this very image: “Surely I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother.” A nursing child clings to its mother out of desperate need for food; a weaned child sits with its mother simply because of who she is. Hannah’s journey traces that same change. She first came to God needing what He could give her, a baby. By the end, she was resting in God so completely that she could give the baby back. The weaning was not only Samuel’s; it was Hannah’s. We cannot fully dedicate our ministries or blessings to God until we are weaned from our fleshly attachment to them. We must reach the point where the Giver is more precious than the gift, where we come to Him not for the milk but for Himself.
items.q: In verse 22 Hannah refuses to go up to the house of the LORD until the child is weaned.

1.brief: The narrative opens by introducing Elkanah, a man of Ramathaim Zophim in the mountains of Ephraim, whose ancestry is traced back four generations to Zuph. God’s work in this book begins within a particular Israelite household rooted in a real place and family.
1.explain:
“Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim,”

First Samuel opens the way several stories in Judges do, with “a certain man” from a particular town (compare Judges 13:2; 17:1). The book that will tell of prophets and kings begins in an ordinary household. “Ramathaim Zophim” is the full name of the town later called Ramah (1:19; 2:11). The name means ‘the two heights,’ and “Zophim” probably ties the place to the family's ancestor Zuph, named at the end of the verse. Ramah became Samuel's home base for the rest of his life; he judged Israel there and built an altar to the LORD there (7:17).

“of the mountains of Ephraim,”

The town lay in the hill country of Ephraim, the central highlands north of Jerusalem. Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, was in the same region, a journey of perhaps a day or two on foot.

“and his name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph,”

The narrator traces “Elkanah” back four generations to “Zuph.” An ancestry this full is usually given for someone whose family matters to the story. Elkanah's name means ‘God has created’ or ‘God has acquired.’ The genealogy roots the beginning of God's work in a real family with a remembered past. Nothing here is legend; God's purposes for Israel begin in a home whose ancestors could be named.

“an Ephraimite.”

The final description places Elkanah in Ephraim. Chronicles lists Samuel's family among the Levites, descendants of Kohath, and names the same ancestors under slightly different forms (1 Chronicles 6:26–27, 33–35). The best explanation is that Elkanah belonged to a Levitical family living in the territory of Ephraim. Levites did not receive a tribal territory of their own; they lived in towns scattered among the other tribes, and the Kohathites were given towns in Ephraim (Joshua 21:20–21). Judges speaks of Levites living “in the remote mountains of Ephraim” (Judges 19:1). “Ephraimite” therefore identifies where the family lived, while Chronicles identifies its tribe.
1.notes:
Chronicles gives Samuel's ancestry twice. 1 Chronicles 6:26–27 reads Zophai, Nahath, Eliab, Jeroham, Elkanah, and 1 Chronicles 6:33–35 reads Zuph, Toah, Eliel, Jeroham, Elkanah, Samuel.

Toah and Nahath correspond to Tohu here, and Eliel and Eliab to Elihu. Such variation in name forms is common between genealogical records.

Some interpreters take “an Ephraimite” to mean that the family was Ephraimite by ancestry and that Chronicles later placed Samuel among the Levites because of his service. Chronicles presents a Levitical descent, and the Hebrew term can describe residence, so a Levitical family living in Ephraim fits both texts.

Heman the singer, one of the leaders of worship David appointed, was Samuel's grandson (1 Chronicles 6:33).

Ramathaim Zophim is commonly identified with Ramah, Samuel's later home (1:19). The exact site of the town is debated.

reflections.title: Born on the Heights of the Watchers
reflections.html: Samuel’s family comes from Ramathaim-zophim, a name rendered “the double heights of the watchers.” Before Israel ever heard a prophet, God was already at work in a town whose very name speaks of watching. True spiritual authority is birthed in the hidden heights of prayer and watchfulness, far from the religious machinery of the day. God loves to begin His new movements in the ordinary, unnoticed lives of those who dwell on the heights and keep watch.
reflections.q: Samuel’s family comes from Ramathaim-zophim, a name rendered “the double heights of the watchers.”

reflections.title: The Importance of Hidden Faithfulness
reflections.html: The “nobodies” of Ephraim become the incubators for national revival. God often begins His greatest works in places the world barely notices.
reflections.q: The “nobodies” of Ephraim become the incubators for national revival.

2.brief: Elkanah has two wives, and the verse sets them in painful contrast: Peninnah has children, but Hannah has none. This difference creates the tension that the rest of the chapter will resolve.
2.explain:
“And he had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah.”

Elkanah had two wives. Scripture records polygamy among Israel's ancestors without commending it, and the households that practiced it are regularly marked by rivalry and grief, as with Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16:4) and Rachel and Leah (Genesis 29:31; 30:1). “Hannah” is named first, which may suggest she was the first wife or the more loved. Her name means ‘grace’ or ‘favor.’ “Peninnah” may mean ‘pearl’ or ‘coral,’ though the meaning is uncertain.

“Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.”

The verse ends with a sharp contrast. In Israel, children were a sign of God's blessing and the hope of a family's future. A woman without children often carried shame as well as sorrow. The words “Hannah had no children” set the problem the chapter will resolve. Scripture repeatedly begins God's great acts with a barren woman: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Samson's mother (Genesis 25:21; Judges 13:2). The pattern shows that the child who comes is God's gift, not human achievement.
2.notes: The Hebrew wording ‘the name of one... the name of the other’ is a common way of introducing two people. It does not by itself establish which wife Elkanah married first.

reflections.title: The Flesh and the Spirit in One House
reflections.html: Peninnah has children; Hannah has none. The scene mirrors Paul’s allegory of Hagar and Sarah (Galatians 4:21–31). Peninnah represents the fruitfulness of the natural: easy, immediate, and abundant. Hannah represents the promise of the Spirit: barren at first, requiring a miracle, and finally bringing forth the seed of destiny. The same two women live in our own house. The flesh produces quickly what everyone can see; the Spirit forms slowly what God has promised. The question is which one we are measuring ourselves by.
reflections.q: Peninnah has children; Hannah has none.

reflections.title: Do Not Measure Favor by What Is Seen
reflections.html: Peninnah’s full household did not prove that she was more favored, and Hannah’s empty arms did not prove that she was forgotten. Do not measure divine favor by immediate, visible productivity. We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen (2 Corinthians 4:18).
reflections.q: Peninnah’s full household did not prove that she was more favored, and Hannah’s empty arms did not prove that she was forgotten.

reflections.title: Barrenness That Creates Dependence
reflections.html: God intentionally uses the barrenness of the natural to create a desperate dependency on the supernatural.
reflections.q: God intentionally uses the barrenness of the natural to create a desperate dependency on the supernatural.

reflections.title: Embrace the Barren Season
reflections.html: The believer must embrace the “barren” seasons when human effort fails, knowing that Christ is forming a deeper, more enduring fruit within.
reflections.q: The believer must embrace the “barren” seasons when human effort fails, knowing that Christ is forming a deeper, more enduring fruit within.

reflections.title: When Custom Replaces God’s Order in the Home
reflections.html: Elkanah’s two wives reflect the customs of his day rather than God’s design for marriage. When we allow the values of the surrounding culture, or what simply seems right in our own eyes, to replace God’s revealed order in our homes, trouble is sure to follow, and the grief of this household begins right here. His Word, rather than the customs around us, must govern the life of the home.
reflections.q: Elkanah’s two wives reflect the customs of his day rather than God’s design for marriage.

3.brief: Elkanah faithfully goes up from his city each year to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. The note that Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas serve there as priests introduces the men whose conduct will soon come under the LORD’s judgment.
3.explain:
“This man went up from his city yearly to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of hosts in Shiloh.”

Elkanah was faithful in worship. He “went up” each year from Ramah to “Shiloh,” where the tabernacle had stood since Joshua's day (Joshua 18:1). The Law called Israelite men to appear before the LORD three times a year (Deuteronomy 16:16). Whether Elkanah's yearly visit was one of these feasts or a special family sacrifice is not stated. What matters is that he went “to worship and sacrifice.” In a period when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25), this household kept going up to the LORD.

“The LORD of hosts” presents God as commander of the armies of heaven and ruler over every power. This is the first time in the order of the biblical books that God is called by this title. It will appear again in Hannah's prayer (1:11), in connection with the ark (4:4), and on David's lips as he faces Goliath (17:45). The household's worship was directed to the sovereign King of all.

“Also the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests of the LORD, were there.”

The narrator adds a note that seems minor but will become central. “Hophni and Phinehas” were Eli's sons and served as “the priests of the LORD” at Shiloh. The title is accurate, but the following chapter will show how badly they dishonored it (2:12–17). From the opening verses, the reader sees both the faithful worshiper and the unfaithful priests at the same sanctuary.
3.notes:
The Hebrew phrase behind “LORD of hosts” joins God's personal name, YHWH (shown in the NKJV as “LORD”), with tseva'ot, the plural of the Hebrew word for an army. The same word is used of Israel's armies, of the heavenly beings who serve God, and of the sun, moon, and stars, so the title presents the LORD as commander of every host in heaven and on earth. This verse is the first place the title appears in the Bible's order of books.

Hophni and Phinehas are generally regarded as names of Egyptian origin. Phinehas is usually traced to the Egyptian name Pa-nehesy, ‘the Nubian’ or ‘the dark-skinned one.’

The same name belonged to Aaron's grandson (Numbers 25:7–13), a different person from Eli's son.

Shiloh lay north of Bethel in Ephraim (Judges 21:19). By this time the sanctuary had doors and doorposts (1:9; 3:15) and is called “the house of the LORD” (1:7), suggesting a more permanent structure around or alongside the tent.

reflections.title: The First Revelation of “the LORD of Hosts”
reflections.html: This verse marks the first time in Scripture that God is called Jehovah Sabaoth, the LORD of Hosts, the LORD of Armies. It is striking that this militant, sovereign title is first spoken not on a bloody battlefield by a king or general, but in the setting of a family’s yearly worship and a barren woman’s private anguish. The LORD’s heavenly armies are engaged in the intimate, quiet battles of our personal lives.
reflections.q: This verse marks the first time in Scripture that God is called Jehovah Sabaoth, the LORD of Hosts, the LORD of Armies.

reflections.title: Faithfulness in the Midst of Institutional Decay
reflections.html: Elkanah kept going up to Shiloh to worship even though Hophni and Phinehas, the priests serving there, were deeply corrupt. We must be careful not to use the weaknesses of spiritual leaders as an excuse to withdraw from the life of the church. Our commitment to gather with God’s people is rooted in devotion to Christ, not in the worthiness of those who lead. Look past the failures of human leaders to the Head of the Church, Christ, the true High Priest.
reflections.q: Elkanah kept going up to Shiloh to worship even though Hophni and Phinehas, the priests serving there, were deeply corrupt.

reflections.title: The LORD Still Reigns When His Representatives Fail
reflections.html: God remains the LORD of Hosts, reigning supreme, even when His earthly representatives fail. The corruption at the altar never touches the authority of the throne.
reflections.q: God remains the LORD of Hosts, reigning supreme, even when His earthly representatives fail.

reflections.title: Sovereign Power Revealed in the Darkest Hour
reflections.html: The title “LORD of hosts” is introduced in the same verse that names Hophni and Phinehas. God reveals His martial, sovereign power at the darkest hour of the priesthood, just as a woman’s intercession is about to begin.
reflections.q: The title “LORD of hosts” is introduced in the same verse that names Hophni and Phinehas.

4.brief: At the sacrificial meal Elkanah gives portions to Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. The ordinary custom of sharing the offering makes the size of Peninnah’s family plain to everyone at the table.
4.explain:
“And whenever the time came for Elkanah to make an offering,”

The scene is the yearly sacrifice at Shiloh. The kind of offering described here was a peace offering, in which part of the animal was burned on the altar, part given to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshiper's family in a meal before the LORD (Leviticus 7:31–34).

“he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.”

At the meal Elkanah distributed portions of the sacrificial meat. Peninnah received her share, and so did “all her sons and daughters,” one by one. The ordinary custom of sharing the offering made the size of Peninnah's family plain to everyone at the table. Each portion handed out was a reminder to Hannah of what she did not have. The feast that should have been a joy became, year after year, the setting of her pain.

reflections.title: Rivalries Acted Out at the Altar
reflections.html: The portions were handed out on the day Elkanah sacrificed. Religious routines can become the very stage where our deepest insecurities and rivalries are acted out.
reflections.q: The portions were handed out on the day Elkanah sacrificed.

reflections.title: The Economy of Natural Provision
reflections.html: Every son and every daughter received a portion, yet nothing on that table could fill what was empty in Hannah. The careful distribution of earthly portions only highlights how inadequate natural provision is to satisfy spiritual emptiness.
reflections.q: Every son and every daughter received a portion, yet nothing on that table could fill what was empty in Hannah.

5.brief: Elkanah gives Hannah a double portion because he loves her, even though the LORD had closed her womb. The verse sets a husband’s real love beside a sorrow that only the LORD can address.
5.explain:
“But to Hannah he would give a double portion,”

Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion. “A double portion” marked her as honored and loved. Elkanah was trying to show publicly that Hannah's barrenness did not lessen her place in his heart.

“for he loved Hannah,”

The narrator explains his motive plainly: “he loved Hannah.” His love was real, and Scripture does not criticize it.

“although the LORD had closed her womb.”

The verse ends with the deeper reality. “The LORD had closed her womb.” The narrator does not attribute Hannah's barrenness to chance or to some hidden sin. It lay under the LORD's sovereign hand. That is both the hardest and the most hopeful part of the verse. If the LORD had closed her womb, then only the LORD could open it. Elkanah's love was genuine, but it could not reach the place where Hannah's sorrow lay.
5.notes:
The Hebrew expression behind “a double portion” is unusual and difficult. It reads literally ‘one portion of two faces,’ and translators have understood it as a double portion, a specially honored portion, or a single portion.

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads that Elkanah gave Hannah ‘a single portion, because she had no child,’ even though he loved her. The NKJV's “double portion” follows the traditional Hebrew text, as do the KJV, NASB, ESV, and NIV; the NLT follows the other understanding with ‘only one choice portion.’

The double share of inheritance given to a firstborn son (Deuteronomy 21:17) uses a different Hebrew expression, literally ‘a mouth of two.’

Genesis uses the same kind of language for the LORD opening the womb for Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:31; 30:22) and closing the wombs of Abimelech's household (Genesis 20:18).

reflections.title: Love Exceeding Output
reflections.html: Elkanah gives Hannah a double portion, or a worthy, choice portion, simply because he loved her. His love was not tied to her productivity. This is a beautiful shadow of Christ’s love for His bride: He loves us not for what we produce, but because we are His. We are invited to a table where our portion rests on the finished work of Christ, not on our natural fruitfulness. Grace provides a double portion precisely where there is no performance or fruit to earn it.
reflections.q: Elkanah gives Hannah a double portion, or a worthy, choice portion, simply because he loved her.

reflections.title: The Sovereign Closure of the Womb
reflections.html: The text says plainly, and repeats it in the next verse, that “the LORD had closed her womb.” Hannah’s barrenness was not an accident of nature; it was a divine assignment. God closed her womb in the natural so that He could open her spirit to bring forth something supernatural, and so that the child, when he came, would be recognized entirely as His work. God will sometimes frustrate our natural fruitfulness to press us into a desperate dependency that births a spiritual legacy. Divine barrenness is often the forerunner of divine birthing.
reflections.q: The text says plainly, and repeats it in the next verse, that “the LORD had closed her womb.”

reflections.title: Closings That Drive Us to Christ
reflections.html: God’s intentional closings in our lives are designed to drive us past earthly comforts into desperate communion with Christ.
reflections.q: God’s intentional closings in our lives are designed to drive us past earthly comforts into desperate communion with Christ.

reflections.title: Meat Cannot Satisfy a Longing for a Son
reflections.html: The double portion of meat could not satisfy a woman who wanted a son. Elkanah tried to solve a spiritual crisis with material abundance.
reflections.q: The double portion of meat could not satisfy a woman who wanted a son.

6.brief: Peninnah, called Hannah’s rival, provokes her severely to make her miserable, using her barrenness against her. For the second time the narrator states that the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, keeping her situation under His hand.
6.explain:
“And her rival also provoked her severely,”

Peninnah is called Hannah's “rival.” The Hebrew word describes a co-wife as an adversary. It is related to the word for distress, and the same word is used in the Law's prohibition against marrying a woman's sister as “a rival” (Leviticus 18:18). “Provoked her severely” means she deliberately irritated and taunted Hannah. The rivalry was not a misunderstanding; it was cruelty.

“to make her miserable,”

Peninnah's aim was to hurt. She wanted Hannah to feel her shame. The narrator does not explain Peninnah's motive, though Elkanah's evident love for Hannah may have fed her jealousy.

“because the LORD had closed her womb.”

For the second time the narrator states that “the LORD had closed her womb” (1:5). Peninnah used Hannah's barrenness as a weapon, but the narrator keeps placing it under the LORD's hand. What Peninnah meant as a taunt was a situation God would answer in His time.

reflections.title: Bring the Wound to God
reflections.html: The place of our deepest pain can become the place of our deepest encounter with God. Peninnah meant to wound Hannah, but she could not decide what Hannah would do with that wound. We cannot always choose what others do to us, but we can choose to carry what they have done into the presence of God. There, instead of festering into bitterness, our wounds can become prayer.
reflections.q: The place of our deepest pain can become the place of our deepest encounter with God.

reflections.title: An Attack Aimed at Her Faith
reflections.html: Notice the reason given for the provocation: “because the LORD had closed her womb.” Peninnah likely used Hannah’s own theology against her: “If God loves you, why has He closed your womb?” The provocation was aimed at Hannah’s faith, not just her fertility. The enemy’s sharpest attacks often take what God has allowed and turn it into an accusation against God’s love.
reflections.q: Notice the reason given for the provocation: “because the LORD had closed her womb.”

reflections.title: Mocked for What They Cannot See
reflections.html: In our barrenness we share in the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings (Philippians 3:10), mocked by those who cannot perceive the invisible work of the Spirit.
reflections.q: In our barrenness we share in the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings (Philippians 3:10), mocked by those who cannot perceive the invisible work of the Spirit.

reflections.title: Beware of Comparison
reflections.html: Peninnah had children and much to be thankful for, yet comparison with Hannah seems to have turned her blessing into rivalry. Comparison moves our eyes off God’s goodness and onto ourselves and others. Receive what God has given you with gratitude, rather than letting someone else’s portion rob you of contentment.
reflections.q: Peninnah had children and much to be thankful for, yet comparison with Hannah seems to have turned her blessing into rivalry.

reflections.title: An Attack Reveals the Attacker’s Heart
reflections.html: Sometimes another person’s attack says more about what is happening inside them than about us. Peninnah’s cruelty, sustained year after year, may have come from a heart that did not know how deeply it was loved. That does not excuse her behavior. But it can help us see those who hurt us differently, and lead us to ask the Father to show us how to pray for them.
reflections.q: Sometimes another person’s attack says more about what is happening inside them than about us.

7.brief: The provocation is not a single incident but happens year after year whenever Hannah goes up to the house of the LORD. The very occasion of worship becomes the time of her deepest grief, so that she weeps and will not eat.
7.explain:
“So it was, year by year,”

The provocation was not a single incident. It happened “year by year.” The repetition stretched Hannah's grief over many years, with each visit renewing the wound.

“when she went up to the house of the LORD, that she provoked her;”

The cruelty came “when she went up to the house of the LORD.” The very occasion of worship became the time of Hannah's deepest grief. Shiloh, the place where Israel met God, was where Peninnah taunted her most.

“therefore she wept and did not eat.”

The result was weeping and refusal to eat. At a feast where everyone ate their portions, Hannah could not. Her grief was so heavy that she could not share the meal. The narrator lets the reader feel the weight of these years before Hannah's prayer is recorded. Her later prayer was not the outburst of a moment but the pouring out of long sorrow.
7.notes: The phrase “the house of the LORD” usually refers to the temple in Jerusalem, but here it describes the sanctuary at Shiloh.

reflections.title: Don’t Let What Others Have Done Keep You From the Lord
reflections.html: People, conflict, and painful experiences among God’s own people can make worship difficult. Year after year, Peninnah’s provocation met Hannah on the very road to the house of the LORD. But we must not let what someone else has done to us keep us from the Lord. Hannah’s answer was not found in Peninnah changing. It was found as Hannah turned toward God and poured out her heart before Him.
reflections.q: People, conflict, and painful experiences among God’s own people can make worship difficult.

reflections.title: Breaking the Year-by-Year Cycle
reflections.html: “Year by year … she wept and did not eat.” Hannah was caught in a cycle of manageable grief. For years she endured her barrenness by weeping and fasting, yet nothing changed. Routine religion without breakthrough becomes a cycle of despair. Weeping over a condition will not change it; only carrying that grief to the altar will. There comes a moment when temporal weeping must turn into a spiritual transaction, when routine provocation must push us out of weeping and into warring. Many in our congregations live in their own “year after year” patterns of defeat; they need to be named and challenged through desperate prayer.
reflections.q: “Year by year … she wept and did not eat.”

reflections.title: No Immunity in the House of the LORD
reflections.html: The house of the LORD provides no automatic immunity from deep personal sorrow.
reflections.q: The house of the LORD provides no automatic immunity from deep personal sorrow.

reflections.title: Attacked on the Way to Worship
reflections.html: The provocation came “when she went up to the house of the LORD.” The enemy strategically attacks believers precisely when they are attempting to approach God.
reflections.q: The provocation came “when she went up to the house of the LORD.”

reflections.title: When Earthly Food Loses Its Appeal
reflections.html: Hannah’s inability to eat points to a loss of appetite for earthly things, a necessary transition before spiritual hunger can fully take over. When earthly food loses its appeal, the soul is being prepared to feed on the Bread of Life alone (John 6:35).
reflections.q: Hannah’s inability to eat points to a loss of appetite for earthly things, a necessary transition before spiritual hunger can fully take over.

8.brief: Elkanah asks why Hannah weeps, why she does not eat, and why her heart is grieved, and whether he is not better to her than ten sons. His love is sincere, but his words show that he cannot meet the deepest longing of her heart.
8.explain:
“Then Elkanah her husband said to her, ‘Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? And why is your heart grieved?’”

Elkanah saw her distress and asked four questions. They show genuine concern. He noticed her tears, her refusal to eat, and her grieved heart. “Your heart” points to her inner life; her grief went to the center of who she was.

“Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

His final question reveals both love and limitation. “Ten sons” expresses a complete and abundant family. Elkanah was saying, in effect, ‘Isn't my love enough?’ His love was sincere, but his words show that he could not meet the deepest longing of her heart. Scripture does not record Hannah's answer. Instead, she rose and went to pray. The one who could meet her need was not Elkanah but the LORD.

1 Samuel 1:9–18 — Hannah’s Prayer and Vow at Shiloh

reflections.title: Love Cannot Supply Everything
reflections.html:
Even the love of those closest to us cannot meet every need of the heart. Elkanah truly loved Hannah, but his love could not give her the child she desired or take away the sorrow she carried. There are places within us that no husband, wife, or friend can fully satisfy, places meant to teach us to look more deeply to the Lord.

Those who love us will not always understand what we are carrying, and their inability to understand does not mean they do not love us. When others cannot grasp what we carry, we can bring it to the Lord, who sees what others cannot see.
reflections.q: Even the love of those closest to us cannot meet every need of the heart.

reflections.title: Sit With the Sorrow
reflections.html: There is a caution here for those who comfort others. Elkanah’s question was sincere, but it could not touch Hannah’s specific ache. Well-meant reassurance that minimizes another person’s grief, however lovingly intended, rarely heals it. Sometimes the more faithful comfort is simply to sit with someone’s sorrow rather than talk them out of it.
reflections.q: There is a caution here for those who comfort others.

reflections.title: Human Affection Cannot Quiet a Divine Ache
reflections.html: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” Elkanah offered his human love as a substitute for what God had placed in Hannah’s heart. His love was genuine, but Hannah was carrying a prophetic burden for fruitfulness that a husband’s love could not extinguish. Human sympathy, however sincere or generous, is radically insufficient for the deep spiritual groan of a soul who knows it was meant to bring forth something for God. We must recognize when human comfort cannot reach a wound only God can heal.
reflections.q: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

reflections.title: A Horizontal Answer to a Vertical Crisis
reflections.html: Elkanah showed genuine affection but deep spiritual tone-deafness. “Ten sons” represented the ultimate ideal of family fulfillment, and yet he made the moment about himself: “Am I not better?” He saw the problem horizontally; Hannah was in a vertical crisis.
reflections.q: Elkanah showed genuine affection but deep spiritual tone-deafness.

reflections.title: Don’t Be Comforted Out of Holy Desperation
reflections.html: Do not let the comfort of loved ones pacify the holy discontent God has placed in you. We must refuse to let the good, human affection, become the enemy of the best, spiritual fruitfulness in Christ. And those of us who care for others must beware of comforting people right out of their divine desperation.
reflections.q: Do not let the comfort of loved ones pacify the holy discontent God has placed in you.

9.brief: After the meal at Shiloh, Hannah rises to go and pray, while Eli the priest sits by the doorpost of the tabernacle of the LORD. The scene moves from the family’s yearly pattern to this particular visit and places Eli where he will observe her.
9.explain:
“So Hannah arose after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh.”

The narrative moves from the yearly pattern to one particular visit. After the meal, “Hannah arose.” The verb marks a turning point. She did not remain at the table in tears; she got up and went to pray. “Eating and drinking” describes the feast that had just ended, and the reference to drinking prepares for Eli's mistaken assumption in verse 13.

“Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat by the doorpost of the tabernacle of the LORD.”

The narrator introduces “Eli the priest.” He was “sitting on the seat,” probably a seat of honor, “by the doorpost of the tabernacle of the LORD.” From that position he could observe all who came to the sanctuary. The word translated “tabernacle” here is the word for a temple or palace, again suggesting a substantial building. Eli's place by the entrance sets him where he will observe Hannah, and his seat will appear again on the day he dies (4:13, 18).
9.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “tabernacle” here usually means a palace or temple, the house of a king. It presents the sanctuary at Shiloh as the dwelling of the LORD as King, and the same word is later used for Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:3).

The Hebrew word for Eli's “seat” is the ordinary word for a chair, and it is also the word for a throne. Here it may point to Eli's official position as priest and judge, though the verse does not explain it.

The Septuagint adds that Hannah stood before the LORD after the meal. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV is shorter.

reflections.title: Nothing Changed Until She Rose to Pray
reflections.html: There are times when nothing changes until we rise to pray. Hannah had wept, stopped eating, and received Elkanah’s attempts to comfort her, but nothing changed until she “arose” to seek the Lord. Her rising marked a shift in both posture and resolve. She left the table of human comfort for the place of divine intervention.
reflections.q: There are times when nothing changes until we rise to pray.

reflections.title: The Rising Woman and the Seated Priest
reflections.html: “Hannah rose … Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat by the doorpost.” The physical contrast carries a spiritual foreshadowing. The word for Eli’s seat is often used of a throne, hinting at his institutional authority alongside his passivity. Eli represents the old, fading religious order: seated, static, comfortable, managing the institution and guarding the doorway, yet possessing no fresh revelation. Hannah represents the new move of the Spirit: rising, desperate, active, pregnant with divine longing and pressing into the presence of God. God was about to bypass the seated priest to answer the rising intercessor.
reflections.q: “Hannah rose … Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat by the doorpost.”

reflections.title: From the Dinner Table to the Altar
reflections.html: Breakthrough begins the moment you stop crying at the dinner table and start crying out at the altar. There is a moment when weeping must turn to wrestling.
reflections.q: Breakthrough begins the moment you stop crying at the dinner table and start crying out at the altar.

reflections.title: One Person’s Prayer Against Systemic Stagnation
reflections.html: Individual initiative in prayer is required to shatter systemic stagnation. Shiloh was stuck; one woman rose.
reflections.q: Individual initiative in prayer is required to shatter systemic stagnation.

reflections.title: Rising to the Great High Priest
reflections.html: The soul must rise from the lower life of emotional despair into the higher life of intercession. The believer must move from passively suffering their condition to actively bringing it before the Great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14–16).
reflections.q: The soul must rise from the lower life of emotional despair into the higher life of intercession.

10.brief: In bitterness of soul Hannah prays to the LORD and weeps in anguish. She brings her grief directly to God rather than hiding it or turning away from Him.
10.explain:
“And she was in bitterness of soul,”

The narrator describes Hannah's inner condition. “Bitterness of soul” describes deep anguish, the bitterness of someone whose life has been emptied. Naomi used the same idea when she asked to be called Mara, ‘bitter’ (Ruth 1:20). Hannah's grief had built up over years of barrenness and provocation.

“and prayed to the LORD”

Hannah took her bitterness to the LORD. She did not hide it, deny it, or turn away from God because of it. She “prayed to the LORD,” the God who had closed her womb (1:5–6) and the only one who could open it. Her prayer did not wait until she felt better. She came in her bitterness.

“and wept in anguish.”

Her prayer came with tears. “Wept in anguish” means she wept bitterly and continuously. Scripture does not treat her tears as a lack of faith. It presents them as part of her prayer. The Psalms invite God's people to “Pour out your heart before Him” (Psalm 62:8), and Hannah did exactly that.

reflections.title: The Holy Use of Bitterness
reflections.html: The phrase translated “greatly distressed” is literally “bitter of soul” (marat nefesh). Hannah did not direct her bitterness at Peninnah or Elkanah; she carried it straight into the presence of the LORD. Unprocessed bitterness becomes poison; bitterness of soul poured out before God becomes intercession. She turned her immense grief into the fuel of her prayer. God’s people need their tears validated and then taught where to take them: toward God rather than toward others.
reflections.q: The phrase translated “greatly distressed” is literally “bitter of soul” (marat nefesh).

reflections.title: The Crucible of Prevailing Intercession
reflections.html: Hannah prayed in bitterness of soul and wept in anguish. True intercession is rarely polite; it is forged in the crucible of soul-agony. Prevailing prayer is not the polished articulation of words but the pouring out of the soul. God sometimes presses a soul into extreme bitterness to squeeze out the true burden of the Spirit. He allowed Hannah’s bitterness to reach a critical mass, so that her prayer would carry enough spiritual weight to shift the history of a nation.
reflections.q: Hannah prayed in bitterness of soul and wept in anguish.

reflections.title: God Does Not Despise Undignified Prayer
reflections.html: Hannah’s prayer was intense, emotional agony, not formal liturgy. God does not despise messy, agonizing, undignified prayer; He responds to it. Authentic prayer often rises from the deepest places of our brokenness.
reflections.q: Hannah’s prayer was intense, emotional agony, not formal liturgy.

reflections.title: Straight Past the Priest
reflections.html: Hannah bypassed Eli entirely. Her desperation tore through the veil of institutional mediation and went directly to the LORD.
reflections.q: Hannah bypassed Eli entirely.

reflections.title: The Spirit Groans With Us
reflections.html: In our deepest distress, the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26), uniting our pain with Christ’s own intercession.
reflections.q: In our deepest distress, the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26), uniting our pain with Christ’s own intercession.

11.brief: Hannah calls on the LORD of hosts to look on her affliction, remember her, and give her a son, and she vows to give that son to the LORD all the days of his life, with no razor coming upon his head. Her vow is understood as a response to God’s leading concerning this child rather than a bargain, although the passage does not record a message from God to her.
11.explain:
“Then she made a vow and said, ‘O LORD of hosts,’”

Hannah's prayer included a “vow,” a solemn promise made to God. She addressed Him as “LORD of hosts,” the title used for His worship at Shiloh (1:3). She called on the sovereign ruler of heaven's armies to act in her small, private grief.

“if You will indeed look on the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, and not forget Your maidservant,”

Hannah asked God to “look on” her affliction, to “remember” her, and not to “forget” her. These are the words of someone who felt unseen. Leah used similar words when she said, “The LORD has surely looked on my affliction” (Genesis 29:32). To “remember” in Scripture means more than recalling; it means to act on someone's behalf, as when God “remembered Noah” (Genesis 8:1) and “remembered Rachel” (Genesis 30:22). Three times she calls herself “Your maidservant,” presenting herself humbly as God's servant.

“but will give Your maidservant a male child,”

Her request was specific: “a male child.”

“then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life,”

Her vow was costly. She would give the son she longed for “to the LORD all the days of his life.” She asked for a son in order to give him back. That is the heart of the verse. Her longing and God's purpose came together in her prayer. Scripture does not record God speaking to Hannah, but the narrative as a whole points to more than a bargain struck in desperation. Her changed face after prayer (1:18), Elkanah's words, “Only let the LORD establish His word” (1:23), and the prophetic reach of her song (2:1–10) together suggest that her prayer became a place where God made something of His purpose known, and her vow was her response to what He was revealing. She wanted a son; God was preparing a prophet.

“and no razor shall come upon his head.”

Hannah added a sign of lifelong consecration. “No razor shall come upon his head” recalls the vow of the Nazirite, whose uncut hair marked him as set apart to the LORD (Numbers 6:5). Samson was dedicated in a similar way from birth (Judges 13:5). Normally a Nazirite vow was temporary; Hannah's son would be set apart for life.
11.notes:
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel does not use the word “Nazirite,” but the promise about the razor resembles the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:2–8).

The Septuagint adds that the child would drink no wine or strong drink. One Hebrew manuscript of Samuel found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran also adds a line at 1:22 about giving the boy as a Nazirite for all time.

Numbers 30:6–15 gave a husband the right to confirm or cancel his wife's vow when he heard it. Elkanah's response in 1:23 shows his consent to Hannah's vow.

reflections.title: Prayer Is Where God Speaks Back
reflections.html: Prayer is a place where God speaks into what we bring before Him. Hannah came carrying her own desperate desire for a son, but she did not leave prayer with only her request lying before God. She heard from Him concerning the purpose He had for the son He would give her, and her vow was her response of agreement, not a bargain. Vows made in the Spirit are not deals struck with heaven; they are a human will coming into line with what God has already purposed.
reflections.q: Prayer is a place where God speaks into what we bring before Him.

reflections.title: Aligning Human Desire With Divine Need
reflections.html: “I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life.” Hannah crossed a threshold here. She asked for a son not to keep him, but to return him. She stopped asking for a child to vindicate herself against Peninnah and asked for one she could give back to God. God needed a prophet; Hannah needed a son. Breakthrough comes when our personal desires intersect with God’s eternal purposes, and when her desire aligned with His kingdom need, the miracle was released. In this she becomes a picture of the Father, willing to offer the son of promise for the redemption of the people.
reflections.q: “I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life.”

reflections.title: Tie Your Request to His Kingdom
reflections.html: If you want to see God answer your prayer, tie your request to His kingdom purposes. Ask not only what you need, but what He is seeking to do through what you are asking for.
reflections.q: If you want to see God answer your prayer, tie your request to His kingdom purposes.

reflections.title: A Prophet God Could Not Get From a Comfortable Woman
reflections.html: Israel was in spiritual decay, and God needed a pure vessel. He used Hannah’s barrenness to bring forth a Nazirite prophet He would not have received from a fertile, comfortable woman. The very lack she begged Him to remove was the thing preparing her to give Him what the nation needed.
reflections.q: Israel was in spiritual decay, and God needed a pure vessel.

reflections.title: The Nazirite Consecration
reflections.html: “No razor shall come upon his head.” Hannah placed the lifelong vow of a Nazirite (Numbers 6) on her unborn child. She was offering her highest and best: a life completely separated to God. This mirrors the absolute consecration of Christ, who lived entirely for the will of the Father, separate from the pollutions of the world. It shows what it truly means for a parent to dedicate a child to God, and it invites us to dedicate our deepest desires entirely to His service.
reflections.q: “No razor shall come upon his head.”

reflections.title: Open Hands
reflections.html: Total surrender, giving the child back before he is even conceived, is the ultimate expression of union with Christ. We hold every blessing with open hands.
reflections.q: Total surrender, giving the child back before he is even conceived, is the ultimate expression of union with Christ.

reflections.title: Appealing to the LORD of Hosts
reflections.html: Hannah addressed God as “LORD of hosts,” appealing to His supreme authority. A powerless woman reached for the highest title of command.
reflections.q: Hannah addressed God as “LORD of hosts,” appealing to His supreme authority.

12.brief: Hannah keeps on praying before the LORD, and Eli watches her mouth. His attention to what he can outwardly see sets up the misunderstanding that follows.
12.explain:
“And it happened, as she continued praying before the LORD,”

Hannah's prayer was not brief. “She continued praying” shows that she remained before God for a long time. Her prayer was “before the LORD,” in His presence at the sanctuary. She was not speaking to Eli or to the people around her.

“that Eli watched her mouth.”

Meanwhile, “Eli watched her mouth.” The priest observed her outward appearance. His attention fixed on what he could see, her moving lips, rather than on what was happening between Hannah and God. This sets up the misunderstanding that follows.

reflections.title: Before the LORD, Not Before People
reflections.html:
Hannah’s prayer was “before the LORD.” She came to meet with God and pour out her heart to Him, not to be heard, noticed, or approved by others, even when Eli misunderstood her.

Concern about the opinions of others can hinder honest prayer. We can become too aware of how we sound or how we appear. But prayer is not a performance for people; it is fellowship with God. When we are truly “before the LORD,” our attention moves from those around us to the One we came to meet.
reflections.q: Hannah’s prayer was “before the LORD.”

reflections.title: Multiplied Prayer
reflections.html: “As she continued praying” can be read literally as “she multiplied her praying.” Hannah did not offer a passing request; she lingered in the presence of God in prolonged, enduring prayer. Breakthrough often requires sustained abiding in the place of agonizing intercession, refusing to leave the altar until the transaction in the spirit is complete.
reflections.q: “As she continued praying” can be read literally as “she multiplied her praying.”

reflections.title: Watching the Mouth, Missing the Heart
reflections.html: Eli was watching her mouth. The religious professional was an observer, not a participant, and the burning prayer of the laywoman stood in sharp contrast to the cold, critical gaze of the high priest. Eli was evaluating the external; God was watching her heart.
reflections.q: Eli was watching her mouth.

reflections.title: Watchers of Mouths
reflections.html: Leaders must not become watchers of mouths rather than participants in the Spirit’s burden.
reflections.q: Leaders must not become watchers of mouths rather than participants in the Spirit’s burden.

reflections.title: When Intercession Looks Abnormal
reflections.html: True intercession often looks abnormal or extreme to those comfortable in religious routine. The institutional church can deeply misunderstand the moving of the Spirit and view it with suspicion. Do not expect religious professionals always to understand your spiritual desperation.
reflections.q: True intercession often looks abnormal or extreme to those comfortable in religious routine.

reflections.title: Willing to Look Foolish
reflections.html: The believer abiding in Christ must be willing to look foolish to the world, and even to the church, in the pursuit of God.
reflections.q: The believer abiding in Christ must be willing to look foolish to the world, and even to the church, in the pursuit of God.

13.brief: Hannah is praying in her heart, with her lips moving but her voice unheard. Seeing only these outward signs, Eli concludes that she is drunk.
13.explain:
“Now Hannah spoke in her heart;”

The narrator explains what Eli could not see. “Hannah spoke in her heart.” Her prayer was inward, directed to God from the depths of her being. In the ancient world prayer was usually spoken aloud, so silent prayer was unusual.

“only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.”

Her lips moved, but no sound came. This was the prayer of someone too deeply moved to speak aloud, pouring out her heart in words only God could hear.

“Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.”

Eli drew the wrong conclusion. Seeing only the outward signs, he assumed “she was drunk.” Feasts at Shiloh could involve drinking (1:9), and Judges records dancing and festivity there (Judges 21:19–21), so drunkenness at the sanctuary may not have been unheard of. Eli's mistake was understandable on the surface, but it showed that he could not discern what was before him. The priest at Shiloh mistook the most earnest prayer in the sanctuary for drunkenness, while his own sons were defiling the sanctuary in plain sight (2:12–17, 22).

reflections.title: The Silent Prayer God Heard
reflections.html: “Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.” Eli heard nothing, but God heard everything. In a world where prayer was usually spoken aloud, Hannah’s silent prayer stood out. The thoughts of our hearts are heard as clearly in heaven as the words of our mouths. The volume of a prayer is not the measure of its depth; the depth of prayer is measured by the engagement of the heart. There are times when sorrow is too deep to say much aloud, but silence does not keep God from hearing us. Often the heart speaks loudest when the voice is silent.
reflections.q: “Hannah spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.”

reflections.title: The Flesh Misreads the Spirit
reflections.html: Eli thought she was drunk. Deep, Spirit-led, agonizing prayer is frequently misunderstood by those accustomed only to formal or superficial religion. The religious system Eli represented lacked the discernment to recognize the deep, groaning work of the Spirit (Romans 8:26). Carnal leadership will often mislabel spiritual desperation as intoxication or disorder, just as the crowd at Pentecost mistook Spirit-filled believers for men full of new wine (Acts 2:13). The deep, silent communion of the inner life is often mistaken by the natural man for drunkenness or madness. The believer must be prepared to look foolish, or be misjudged by the religious establishment, when travailing in the Spirit.
reflections.q: Eli thought she was drunk.

reflections.title: Slow to Judge What We Do Not Understand
reflections.html: Spiritual leadership requires more than seeing what is happening outwardly; it requires discernment. Eli saw Hannah’s moving lips and wrongly concluded she was drunk. Intense, travailing prayer has often been misread by onlookers throughout the history of the church. We should be slow to judge what we do not understand.
reflections.q: Spiritual leadership requires more than seeing what is happening outwardly; it requires discernment.

reflections.title: Projecting His Sons’ Sins
reflections.html: Eli was accustomed to the corrupt behavior of his own sons, Hophni and Phinehas, at the sanctuary, and he projected their fleshly conduct onto Hannah’s spiritual agony. What we tolerate around us shapes what we expect to see in others.
reflections.q: Eli was accustomed to the corrupt behavior of his own sons, Hophni and Phinehas, at the sanctuary, and he projected their fleshly conduct onto Hannah’s spiritual agony.

reflections.title: Familiarity Is Not Knowing God
reflections.html: Being around the things of God does not make us spiritual. Eli lived and served at the very center of Israel’s worship, yet he mistook a woman pouring out her heart to God for someone who was drunk. Familiarity with the things of God must never become a substitute for knowing God Himself.
reflections.q: Being around the things of God does not make us spiritual.

reflections.title: Communion Beyond Words
reflections.html: The indwelling Christ communicates with the Father through the believer in ways that go beyond human language. Prayer of the heart moves beyond written lists into deep, inward communion.
reflections.q: The indwelling Christ communicates with the Father through the believer in ways that go beyond human language.

14.brief: Eli rebukes Hannah as though she were drunk and tells her to put away her wine. The priest at Shiloh misjudges a woman in sincere prayer, showing that holding religious office does not guarantee discernment.
14.explain:
“So Eli said to her, ‘How long will you be drunk?’”

Eli rebuked Hannah harshly. “How long will you be drunk?” assumed that she had been drinking for some time and was continuing to make a spectacle at the sanctuary.

“Put your wine away from you!”

He ordered her to stop drinking. The command may mean ‘sober up’ or ‘get rid of your wine.’ The Law forbade priests to drink wine when they entered the tabernacle (Leviticus 10:9), and Eli may have felt responsible for keeping drunkenness away from the sanctuary. But he had misread the situation completely. The priest at Shiloh misjudged a woman in sincere prayer, showing that holding religious office does not guarantee discernment. Hannah, who had come to God in bitterness, was now accused by the priest.

reflections.title: Tolerating Wolves, Attacking Sheep
reflections.html: Eli, who failed to restrain his own sons’ open wickedness, was quick to falsely accuse a righteous woman of drunkenness. The man who should have been interceding for the people was instead accusing the only true intercessor in Shiloh. His inability to tell the groaning of the Spirit from the effects of wine exposes the spiritual bankruptcy of the place.
