When spiritual leaders lose their discernment, they tolerate wolves but attack the sheep. That Hannah endured this false accusation without losing her focus on God is a mark of profound spiritual maturity.
reflections.q: Eli, who failed to restrain his own sons’ open wickedness, was quick to falsely accuse a righteous woman of drunkenness.

reflections.title: Let the Lord Search Us First
reflections.html: Eli was quick to correct Hannah for what he thought was wrong, while later chapters reveal that he failed to deal firmly with the serious sins of his own sons (1 Samuel 2:12–17, 22–25; 3:13). It is easier to see what we think is wrong in someone else than to face what God wants to correct in us. Before we rush to correct someone else, we should let the Lord search our own hearts.
reflections.q: Eli was quick to correct Hannah for what he thought was wrong, while later chapters reveal that he failed to deal firmly with the serious sins of his own sons (1 Samuel 2:12–17, 22–25; 3:13).

reflections.title: The Rebuke of the Blind Watchman
reflections.html: “Put away your wine from you.” Eli’s rebuke was harsh, inaccurate, and based on superficial observation. When we are carrying a burden from the Lord, we must be prepared to be misunderstood, criticized, or even falsely accused by the very leaders who should be guiding us. Hannah’s response would shape her breakthrough: she did not become offended, but stayed focused on God.
reflections.q: “Put away your wine from you.”

reflections.title: Discernment Needs More Than Eyesight
reflections.html: The natural mind cannot understand the things of the Spirit and often mislabels spiritual intensity as fleshly excess. Spiritual discernment requires more than physical eyesight; it requires the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
reflections.q: The natural mind cannot understand the things of the Spirit and often mislabels spiritual intensity as fleshly excess.

reflections.title: The True Judge Knows
reflections.html: When falsely accused, the believer can rest in the reality that Christ, the true Judge, knows the purity of their motives.
reflections.q: When falsely accused, the believer can rest in the reality that Christ, the true Judge, knows the purity of their motives.

reflections.title: Listen Before Correcting
reflections.html: Leaders must learn to listen before they correct.
reflections.q: Leaders must learn to listen before they correct.

15.brief: Hannah respectfully denies drinking wine or strong drink and explains that she is a woman of sorrowful spirit who has poured out her soul before the LORD. Her answer describes her prayer as the honest emptying of her heart before God.
15.explain:
“But Hannah answered and said, ‘No, my lord,’”

Hannah answered respectfully. “No, my lord” denied the accusation while honoring Eli's position. She did not lash out at him, even though she had been wrongly accused.

“I am a woman of sorrowful spirit.”

She explained her condition. “A woman of sorrowful spirit” describes someone burdened in spirit, weighed down by grief. Her moving lips came from sorrow, not from wine.

“I have drunk neither wine nor intoxicating drink,”

She denied drinking anything, wine or any other intoxicating drink. The words recall the Nazirite's abstinence (Numbers 6:3).

“but have poured out my soul before the LORD.”

Her answer describes her prayer as the honest emptying of her heart before God. “Poured out my soul” pictures liquid emptied from a vessel until nothing remains. Lamentations uses the same image: “Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord” (Lamentations 2:19). Hannah had held nothing back. She had given God her sorrow, her longing, and her vow.
15.notes:
The Hebrew behind “a woman of sorrowful spirit” reads literally ‘a woman hard of spirit.’ The word ‘hard’ can also mean severe or harsh, and here it describes a spirit weighed down by long trouble.

The Hebrew verb behind “poured out” is the ordinary word for pouring out water or other liquids. The Psalms use the same verb for pouring out one's heart or complaint to God (Psalm 62:8; 142:2), which is what Hannah says she has been doing.

reflections.title: Honor Without Surrendering the Truth
reflections.html: Being wrongly judged does not give us permission to respond wrongly. Hannah did not accept Eli’s false accusation, but neither did she answer with anger or turn his own household’s failures against him. She did not attack the priest; she humbly and clearly explained her spiritual state. Her answer joined honor with courage. We can speak the truth clearly, with humble clarity rather than defensive rage, without retaliating or dishonoring the one who wronged us.
reflections.q: Being wrongly judged does not give us permission to respond wrongly.

reflections.title: Pouring Out the Soul
reflections.html: “I have poured out my soul before the LORD.” This phrase (shafakh nefesh) becomes a lasting biblical picture of deep, emptying prayer (Psalm 62:8). True prayer is not merely the recitation of words. It is emptying our anxieties, desires, and griefs into the hands of God, emptying the vessel of self so it can be filled with divine purpose. That emptying creates room for the Holy Spirit to fill. To pour out the soul is to hold nothing back, edit nothing, and hide nothing from God.
reflections.q: “I have poured out my soul before the LORD.”

reflections.title: Wine Poured or a Soul Poured
reflections.html: Eli accused her of drinking wine; Hannah answered that she had poured out her soul. Set the two side by side: the pouring of wine in fleshly indulgence and the pouring of a soul in spiritual sacrifice. Hannah was, in effect, offering herself as a drink offering before the LORD.
reflections.q: Eli accused her of drinking wine; Hannah answered that she had poured out her soul.

reflections.title: The Poured-Out Soul
reflections.html: Hannah’s poured-out soul foreshadows the self-emptying of Christ (Philippians 2:7) and His pouring out of His soul unto death (Isaiah 53:12). Believers are called to pour out their lives like a drink offering, just as Christ poured out His soul. True spiritual fruitfulness requires the total emptying of the self.
reflections.q: Hannah’s poured-out soul foreshadows the self-emptying of Christ (Philippians 2:7) and His pouring out of His soul unto death (Isaiah 53:12).

16.brief: Hannah asks Eli not to regard her as a wicked woman, because she has been speaking out of the abundance of her complaint and grief. She defends her character while openly acknowledging the depth of her distress.
16.explain:
“Do not consider your maidservant a wicked woman,”

Hannah asked Eli not to regard her as “a wicked woman.” The Hebrew expression is literally ‘a daughter of Belial,’ meaning a worthless or wicked person. The irony is sharp. The same expression describes Eli's sons, who are called ‘sons of Belial’ (translated “corrupt” in 2:12). Eli suspected a godly woman of being worthless, while his own sons were the worthless ones serving at the altar.

“for out of the abundance of my complaint and grief I have spoken until now.”

Hannah explained that she had been speaking “out of the abundance of my complaint and grief.” “Complaint” here means her troubled thoughts, the burden she had poured out to God. “Grief” describes the provocation and sorrow she had endured. She defended her character while openly acknowledging the depth of her distress. Scripture does not rebuke her for bringing her complaint to God. Her prayer was honest, and God received it.
16.notes: Behind “wicked woman” is the Hebrew phrase ‘a daughter of beliyya'al.’ The word beliyya'al means worthlessness and is used in the Old Testament for people who are base and wicked. Phrases built on the same word, ‘sons of beliyya'al’ or ‘son of beliyya'al,’ appear in Deuteronomy 13:13, Judges 19:22, and 1 Samuel 25:17, where the NKJV renders them “corrupt men,” “perverted men,” and “such a scoundrel.” Hannah is asking Eli not to count her among such people.

reflections.title: The Irony of a “Daughter of Belial”
reflections.html: The phrase “worthless woman” is literally “daughter of Belial,” the same term later used to describe Eli’s own sons (1 Samuel 2:12). The irony is staggering. Eli was ready to label Hannah a daughter of Belial, while his own sons were the true sons of Belial. The woman he suspected of wickedness was the most righteous person in the chapter.
reflections.q: The phrase “worthless woman” is literally “daughter of Belial,” the same term later used to describe Eli’s own sons (1 Samuel 2:12).

reflections.title: Rejecting the Labels of a Broken System
reflections.html: “Do not consider your maidservant a wicked woman.” Hannah respectfully but firmly rejected Eli’s false judgment. She refused to let her agony be categorized as wickedness. In the place of prayer she guarded her identity, refusing to absorb the condemnation of a spiritually blind priest.
reflections.q: “Do not consider your maidservant a wicked woman.”

reflections.title: Grace Under Provocation
reflections.html: Hannah could have reacted to Eli’s insulting accusation with offense and anger. Instead she answered with deep respect, “No, my lord,” and honest vulnerability. Refusing to take offense at spiritual leadership, even when it is wrong, keeps our hearts pure and our prayers unhindered.
reflections.q: Hannah could have reacted to Eli’s insulting accusation with offense and anger.

reflections.title: Anguish in Prayer Is Not Sin
reflections.html: It is not a sin to express profound grief and frustration to God. Emotional anguish in prayer is a legitimate and holy biblical practice. Grief and provocation, when directed toward the throne of grace, are signs not of spiritual worthlessness but of spiritual depth.
reflections.q: It is not a sin to express profound grief and frustration to God.

reflections.title: He Understands Our Provocation
reflections.html: Christ understands the “great concern and provocation” of living in a fallen world, and He invites us to cast all our anxieties on Him (1 Peter 5:7).
reflections.q: Christ understands the “great concern and provocation” of living in a fallen world, and He invites us to cast all our anxieties on Him (1 Peter 5:7).

reflections.title: Teach People to Pray Their Pain
reflections.html: The church must remove the stigma from emotional anguish and teach people how to pray their pain.
reflections.q: The church must remove the stigma from emotional anguish and teach people how to pray their pain.

17.brief: Eli now sends Hannah away in peace and asks that the God of Israel grant the petition she has made of Him. The priest who misjudged her becomes the one who blesses her request.
17.explain:
“Then Eli answered and said, ‘Go in peace,’”

Eli's attitude changed. Having heard Hannah's explanation, he sent her away with a blessing. “Go in peace” was a common farewell, but from the priest it carried the weight of a blessing given at the sanctuary.

“and the God of Israel grant your petition which you have asked of Him.”

Eli asked that “the God of Israel” would grant her petition. He did not know what she had asked, but he prayed that God would answer. The priest who misjudged her became the one who blessed her request. The words “petition” and “asked” come from the Hebrew root meaning ‘to ask,’ which will run through the rest of the chapter and sound in Samuel's name (1:20, 27–28).
17.notes:
The Hebrew verb sha'al, ‘to ask,’ lies behind both “petition” and “asked” in Eli's words. The same word group returns in 1:20, 27, and 28.

The name Saul (Hebrew Sha'ul) is spelled exactly like a form of this verb that means ‘asked for’ (1:28). The same verb is used again when the people ask for a king (8:10; 12:13, where the NKJV renders it “desired”).

“Grant” can be read as a wish (‘may He grant’) or a promise (‘He will grant’), because the Hebrew verb form allows either. Most translations take it as a wish, and the NKJV's wording reads it as a blessing.

reflections.title: The Accidental Prophecy of a Fading Priest
reflections.html: “Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition.” Eli did not even know what Hannah had asked for, yet he released an authoritative blessing. God used Eli’s blind blessing to confirm her specific request. The power was not in Eli’s personal spirituality but in God’s response to Hannah’s faith.
reflections.q: “Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition.”

reflections.title: God Can Speak Through Imperfect People
reflections.html: Eli shifted from accuser to blesser. He was spiritually dull, a poor father, and had just falsely accused her, yet he still occupied the office of priest, and God honored his words. The Lord honors His appointed offices and can speak through flawed and compromised vessels to bring a word of release and comfort to a faithful soul. Receive God’s word of peace even when the messenger is imperfect. Our confidence is not in the vessel, but in the God who can speak and work through imperfect people.
reflections.q: Eli shifted from accuser to blesser.

reflections.title: Our Perfect High Priest Is Our Peace
reflections.html: The word of peace from the altar sealed the transaction of prayer in Hannah’s heart. Christ, our perfect High Priest, not only grants the petition but is Himself the peace that passes all understanding (Philippians 4:7).
reflections.q: The word of peace from the altar sealed the transaction of prayer in Hannah’s heart.

reflections.title: Speak Blessing Over the Brokenhearted
reflections.html: Never underestimate the power of a pastoral blessing spoken over the brokenhearted.
reflections.q: Never underestimate the power of a pastoral blessing spoken over the brokenhearted.

18.brief: Hannah asks to find favor in Eli’s sight, then goes her way, eats, and her face is no longer sad. Her countenance changes before any child is conceived, which supports the understanding that she had received assurance from the LORD in prayer.
18.explain:
“And she said, ‘Let your maidservant find favor in your sight.’”

Hannah responded with humility. She asked to “find favor” in Eli's sight, accepting his blessing with gratitude. The word for “favor” is related to her own name, Hannah, ‘grace.’

“So the woman went her way and ate,”

Hannah left and ate. The woman who had wept and refused to eat at every feast now ate. Something had changed.

“and her face was no longer sad.”

The verse ends with a striking note: “her face was no longer sad.” Nothing had changed in her circumstances. She was not yet pregnant. Peninnah was still her rival. Yet her countenance had changed. Her countenance changed before any child was conceived, which supports the understanding that she had received assurance from the LORD in prayer. She had brought her grief to God, and she left with peace.

1 Samuel 1:19–23 — The LORD Remembers Hannah, and Samuel Is Born

reflections.title: Faith Can Rest Before It Sees
reflections.html: Hannah’s face changed while her circumstances remained the same. The language suggests her very countenance was transformed. This is the shape faith takes before the answer arrives: peace received by trust, not by sight. Her womb was still closed, but faith had something to rest on before it had anything to see. Cast all your care upon Him, for He cares for you (1 Peter 5:7).
reflections.q: Hannah’s face changed while her circumstances remained the same.

reflections.title: The Countenance of Accomplished Faith
reflections.html: “So the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.” This is one of the clearest biblical pictures of faith. Hannah’s countenance changed before she was pregnant, before she went home, before she held a baby. She went in burdened and came out joyful, yet she was no more pregnant on the way out than on the way in. She received the word in her spirit so completely that it altered her behavior and her emotional state before anything physical appeared. Her eating proved her fast was over. When a burden is lifted in the spirit, the outward life comes to rest, because faith treats the transaction as complete.
reflections.q: “So the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.”

reflections.title: Leave the Burden at the Altar
reflections.html: True prayer leaves the burden at the altar; we should not walk away carrying what we just surrendered. Hannah had met with God, poured out her soul before Him, and left what she could not carry in His hands. Then she acted like it: she ate. When we cast our cares on Christ, we must sometimes change what we do, eat the meal, wash our face, to line up with our faith that He has taken the burden.
reflections.q: True prayer leaves the burden at the altar; we should not walk away carrying what we just surrendered.

reflections.title: How to Know You Have Prayed Through
reflections.html: The countenance of faith: there is a way to know when we have prayed through to breakthrough. The face changes before the facts do.
reflections.q: The countenance of faith: there is a way to know when we have prayed through to breakthrough.

19.brief: The family rises early, worships before the LORD, and returns home to Ramah, where Elkanah knows Hannah his wife and the LORD remembers her. The LORD answers the very request she made in verse 11, that He would remember His maidservant.
19.explain:
“Then they rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD,”

The family rose early and worshiped before leaving Shiloh. Hannah worshiped with them, now with a different heart.

“and returned and came to their house at Ramah.”

They went home to “Ramah,” the shorter name of Ramathaim Zophim (1:1).

“And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife,”

“Knew” is the Hebrew way of describing marital union (compare Genesis 4:1).

“and the LORD remembered her.”

The decisive words are “the LORD remembered her.” Hannah had asked God to “remember” her and not forget His maidservant (1:11). Now He did. To “remember” in Scripture means that God acted on her behalf. The LORD who had closed her womb (1:5–6) now opened it. The narrator gives God the credit for the conception, not Elkanah or Hannah.
19.notes: The same verb, “remembered,” is used when God opened Rachel's womb (Genesis 30:22).

reflections.title: When God Remembers, God Moves
reflections.html: “The LORD remembered her.” In Scripture, God’s remembering (zakar) is not Him recalling a forgotten fact, as if He had ever forgotten Hannah. It is Him moving into active covenant fulfillment on her behalf. Divine remembrance is the activation of God’s covenant power in human history. It is an act of intervention, not an exercise of memory.
reflections.q: “The LORD remembered her.”

reflections.title: Worship Before the Answer
reflections.html: Faith worships before circumstances change. Hannah rose early and “worshiped before the LORD” while she was still barren. The order matters: they worshiped, they returned home, and then God acted. True worship happens in the space between the promise and the fulfillment. Worship is not a reward we give God once our prayer is answered; it is a posture we keep regardless of the outcome. Worship God for the answer before you see the evidence.
reflections.q: Faith worships before circumstances change.

reflections.title: Ordinary Union, Divine Remembering
reflections.html: “Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her.” The miracle required both human participation and divine intervention. The union of husband and wife was ordinary, but the spiritual reality behind it was that the LORD remembered. Natural intimacy became the vehicle for a supernatural promise. The natural still needs the breath of the supernatural.
reflections.q: “Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her.”

reflections.title: Trusting God Is Not Passivity
reflections.html: God often works through the ordinary means He has established. Hannah had asked God to do what she could not do, yet the conception came in the normal course of married life. Trusting God does not mean becoming passive. We pray for what only He can do while faithfully doing what He has given us to do.
reflections.q: God often works through the ordinary means He has established.

reflections.title: Life Out of Dead Circumstances
reflections.html: As we walk in union with Christ, His remembering of us brings forth life out of our dead circumstances.
reflections.q: As we walk in union with Christ, His remembering of us brings forth life out of our dead circumstances.

20.brief: In the process of time Hannah conceives and bears a son, and she names him Samuel, saying, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” The child’s name becomes a lasting testimony that he is God’s answer to her prayer.
20.explain:
“So it came to pass in the process of time that Hannah conceived and bore a son,”

The answer came “in the process of time,” literally ‘at the turning of the days.’ The child was conceived and born in God's timing. Hannah “bore a son,” the “male child” she had asked for (1:11).

“and called his name Samuel,”

Hannah named him “Samuel.” In Israel, a mother often named her child, and the name expressed something about his birth.

“saying, ‘Because I have asked for him from the LORD.’”

Hannah explained the name: “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” The child's name became a lasting testimony that he was God's answer to her prayer. Every time someone said his name, they would be reminded that this boy was asked from the LORD and given by Him.
20.notes:
In Hebrew the name Samuel (Shemu'el) is most likely formed from shem, ‘name,’ and El, ‘God,’ so that it means ‘name of God’ or ‘his name is God.’

Hannah's explanation, “I have asked for him,” uses the Hebrew verb sha'al, ‘to ask,’ which sounds similar to the name Samuel but is not the word the name was formed from. Her explanation is a play on similar sounds rather than an account of how the name was originally formed. Biblical name explanations often work by sound and association, as in Genesis 4:1.

reflections.title: The Memorial Name
reflections.html: Hannah named him Samuel, a name that sounds like “heard of God” and that she tied to her asking: “Because I have asked him of the LORD.” The name became a permanent memorial of answered prayer. Every time she called her son, she was testifying to the nature of God as the One who hears desperate prayer. The child’s very identity was wrapped in God’s responsiveness and rooted in his mother’s intercession. Memorialize your breakthroughs, so you never forget that they came by prayer and not by your own effort.
reflections.q: Hannah named him Samuel, a name that sounds like “heard of God” and that she tied to her asking: “Because I have asked him of the LORD.”

reflections.title: A Name That Is Itself a Testimony
reflections.html: Samuel’s name marked him from birth as living evidence of what God had done. Long afterward, another Son received a name not by His mother’s request but by God’s own command, before He was born: “You shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). As Hannah testified every time she spoke Samuel’s name, every time the name of Jesus is spoken it too is a living testimony, not to what was asked of God, but to what God Himself came to do.
reflections.q: Samuel’s name marked him from birth as living evidence of what God had done.

reflections.title: Everything Born of the Spirit Bears Its Origin
reflections.html: Everything birthed by the Spirit carries the mark of its origin. A life birthed in prayer will be a life characterized by hearing God.
reflections.q: Everything birthed by the Spirit carries the mark of its origin.

reflections.title: In Due Time
reflections.html: “In due time” is literally “at the turning of the days.” God fulfills His promises in His exact, appointed timing.
reflections.q: “In due time” is literally “at the turning of the days.”

reflections.title: A Name That Silenced the Mocker
reflections.html: The name Samuel would stand as a lifelong rebuke to Peninnah’s mockery. The child of grace silenced the taunting of the flesh.
reflections.q: The name Samuel would stand as a lifelong rebuke to Peninnah’s mockery.

reflections.title: Children Asked of the Lord
reflections.html: We too are children “asked of the Lord,” born of the Spirit, depending entirely on God’s grace rather than on the will of man (John 1:13).
reflections.q: We too are children “asked of the Lord,” born of the Spirit, depending entirely on God’s grace rather than on the will of man (John 1:13).

reflections.title: Build Spiritual Monuments
reflections.html: Name your seasons and your breakthroughs. They become spiritual monuments for the next generation.
reflections.q: Name your seasons and your breakthroughs.

21.brief: Elkanah goes up with all his household to offer the LORD the yearly sacrifice and his vow. The family’s faithful worship continues, now with the promised son in the household.
21.explain:
“Now the man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and his vow.”

The family's faithful worship continued. Elkanah went up with “all his house” to Shiloh for “the yearly sacrifice.” He also went to offer “his vow.” The text does not say what Elkanah's vow was. He may have made his own vow in connection with the promised son, or he may have been fulfilling a vow of thanksgiving. Either way, the household's worship continued, now with the son God had given in the home. The family that had gone up in sorrow now went up in thanksgiving.
21.notes:
Vows were to be paid without delay (Deuteronomy 23:21).

The Septuagint adds ‘and all the tithes of his land.’ The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV mentions only the yearly sacrifice and his vow.

reflections.title: The Answer Can Test Us Too
reflections.html: Need drove Hannah toward God; answered prayer would reveal whether she would keep her vow. The question now was whether gratitude would become lasting devotion, and whether a commitment made in need would be remembered once the pressure lifted. Blessing can test our surrender as surely as waiting.
reflections.q: Need drove Hannah toward God; answered prayer would reveal whether she would keep her vow.

reflections.title: A Husband Who Believed
reflections.html: Elkanah went up to “pay his vow.” The mention of his vow suggests he had joined Hannah in her commitment, and implies he believed her when she said she had heard from God about giving Samuel to Him for His purposes. Here is a quiet, steady, spiritually supportive husband who honored the spiritual commitments of his household and stood as a true partner in the things of God.
reflections.q: Elkanah went up to “pay his vow.”

reflections.title: Keep Your Daily Obedience After the Answer
reflections.html: Elkanah continued his routine of obedience. When God answers your prayer, do not neglect your ordinary, daily obedience to Him. Routine obedience builds the framework in which radical faith can operate.
reflections.q: Elkanah continued his routine of obedience.

reflections.title: Paying Our Vows
reflections.html: Follow through on the promises you made in the dark once you reach the light. Spiritual leadership in the home includes fulfilling the vows made to God.
reflections.q: Follow through on the promises you made in the dark once you reach the light.

reflections.title: From Private Encounter to Shared Faithfulness
reflections.html: The private miracle was now being carried into the family’s public worship. Our individual encounters with Christ must eventually become shared, corporate faithfulness among His people.
reflections.q: The private miracle was now being carried into the family’s public worship.

22.brief: Hannah does not go up this time, telling her husband that once the child is weaned, likely around age three, she will bring him to appear before the LORD and remain there forever. Her plan shows that she intends to keep her vow completely, giving Samuel to the LORD’s presence for life.
22.explain:
“But Hannah did not go up,”

Hannah stayed home this time. She had good reason.

“for she said to her husband, ‘Not until the child is weaned;’”

She explained that she would wait “until the child is weaned.” In the ancient world, children were often nursed for two to three years. Weaning was a significant moment, sometimes marked by a feast (Genesis 21:8). Hannah planned to keep Samuel with her through these early years.

“then I will take him, that he may appear before the LORD and remain there forever.”

Hannah's plan shows that she intended to keep her vow completely. When Samuel was weaned, she would bring him “that he may appear before the LORD,” a phrase used for Israel's appearing at the sanctuary (Exodus 34:23). He would “remain there forever,” that is, for the rest of his life. Hannah was not looking for a way to delay or reduce her vow. She was preparing to give her son fully.
22.notes:
An ancient Jewish writing outside the Bible, 2 Maccabees, refers to a mother nursing her son for three years, which is consistent with weaning at about two or three years old. The Bible does not give Samuel's age when he was brought to Shiloh.

One Hebrew manuscript of Samuel found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran adds a line at the end of this verse, rendered in the NRSV ‘I will offer him as a nazirite for all time.’ This addition is not in the Hebrew text followed by the NKJV.

Levites normally served at the sanctuary between the ages of twenty-five or thirty and fifty (Numbers 4:3; 8:24–25). Samuel's lifelong service from childhood went beyond that pattern.

reflections.title: The Hidden Incubation Period
reflections.html: “I will not go up until the child is weaned.” Weaning in the ancient world often came around age three. Hannah recognized that a child could not survive in the temple, especially Eli’s corrupted temple, until he was strengthened. New blessings, new believers, new ministries, and new callings need a season of hidden nursing and maturing before they are presented in the public sanctuary. Premature exposure can damage the gift.
reflections.q: “I will not go up until the child is weaned.”

reflections.title: Shiloh Is Now in Her Arms
reflections.html: Hannah did not go to Shiloh, because Shiloh was now in her arms. She was nurturing the future of the nation in her own home. She set aside the temple for a few years so she could give the temple a prophet for a lifetime.
reflections.q: Hannah did not go to Shiloh, because Shiloh was now in her arms.

reflections.title: Separation for Preparation
reflections.html: Elkanah went up with the yearly sacrifice, but Hannah stayed behind. Once the promise was secured, the rhythm of her life changed. She stepped out of the traditional religious routine to do the hidden, essential work of nursing and preparing the promised child. Sometimes the highest spiritual act is staying home and tending the quiet work God has entrusted to you. Faithful stewardship of God’s gifts requires time, patience, and at times separation from our standard routines.
reflections.q: Elkanah went up with the yearly sacrifice, but Hannah stayed behind.

reflections.title: Surrender Does Not Cancel Stewardship
reflections.html: Giving something to God does not mean neglecting the responsibility He has placed in our hands for it. Hannah had promised Samuel to the LORD, but before she could bring him to Shiloh, she had to nurse him and care for him. Surrender does not release us from responsibility; it changes how we understand it. Faithful obedience does not always mean immediate action. Hannah’s timing was wise, not reluctant: she settled when the vow would be fulfilled without abandoning its substance. God’s call can include patient, Spirit-led planning rather than rushing to prove our sincerity.
reflections.q: Giving something to God does not mean neglecting the responsibility He has placed in our hands for it.

reflections.title: A Secret History With Christ
reflections.html: The believer must cultivate a secret history with Christ, nurturing the seed of the Word within before it is ever put on public display.
reflections.q: The believer must cultivate a secret history with Christ, nurturing the seed of the Word within before it is ever put on public display.

reflections.title: Wean the Vision Before You Release It
reflections.html: Do not rush the process of spiritual preparation. Wean the vision properly before you release it publicly.
reflections.q: Do not rush the process of spiritual preparation.

23.brief: Elkanah approves Hannah’s plan and adds, “Only let the LORD establish His word,” and she nurses her son until he is weaned. His words ask the LORD to bring His purpose to completion and leave room for a word from God connected with Hannah’s prayer, though the passage does not say precisely what that word was.
23.explain:
“So Elkanah her husband said to her, ‘Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him.’”

Elkanah agreed with Hannah's plan. “Do what seems best to you” gave her freedom to decide the timing. His consent also confirmed her vow, as the Law allowed a husband to do (Numbers 30:6–8).

“Only let the LORD establish His word.”

Elkanah added a prayer: “Only let the LORD establish His word.” “Establish” means to confirm, to bring to pass, to make stand. Elkanah asked the LORD to fulfill His purpose. The phrase “His word” leaves room for a word from God connected with Hannah's prayer and Samuel's dedication. It may refer to Eli's blessing (1:17), which Elkanah understood as spoken for the LORD, or to a word from the LORD that Hannah had received in prayer. The narrative does not say precisely what that word was. Read with Hannah's changed face (1:18) and her prophetic song (2:1–10), the phrase fits the understanding that God had made something of His purpose for this child known. It supports that inference without establishing the content of a revelation by itself.

“Then the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him.”

Hannah stayed home and “nursed her son until she had weaned him.” These were precious years with the child she would soon give away.
23.notes:
The Hebrew text and the NKJV read “His word.” The Septuagint and a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel from Qumran read ‘what proceeds from your mouth,’ that is, Hannah's vow. In Hebrew the two readings differ by only one letter at the end of the word.

On that reading, Elkanah prays that the LORD will enable Hannah to fulfill what she has promised. The NKJV's “His word” follows the Hebrew.

Even within the Hebrew text, the meaning of “His word” remains open. Eli's blessing (1:17), a word received by Hannah, and God's purpose for Samuel more broadly are all possible.

1 Samuel 1:24–28 — Samuel Lent to the LORD

reflections.title: Marital Unity in Keeping a Vow
reflections.html: “Do what seems best to you … only let the LORD establish His word.” Under the Law, Elkanah had the right to annul his wife’s vow (Numbers 30:6–8). Instead he gave his consent and used his leadership to support and encourage it, becoming her partner rather than her obstacle. There is power in a marriage that comes into agreement with what God is doing. Their unity protected the destiny of the prophet. A home united around the word and purpose of God is the ideal incubator for the prophetic.
reflections.q: “Do what seems best to you … only let the LORD establish His word.”

reflections.title: Support Your Spouse’s Assignment
reflections.html: Support the spiritual assignments of your spouse, even when they interrupt family traditions. Husbands and wives must come into alignment when raising children, and carrying callings, for God’s purposes, and together protect the calling on their household.
reflections.q: Support the spiritual assignments of your spouse, even when they interrupt family traditions.

reflections.title: Only Let the LORD Establish His Word
reflections.html: Elkanah’s final word made God’s word the deciding factor. God’s Word must be the ultimate arbiter in family decisions.
reflections.q: Elkanah’s final word made God’s word the deciding factor.

reflections.title: A Promise They Were Both Holding
reflections.html: “Only let the LORD establish His word.” There was likely a broader promise spoken over this child that both Elkanah and Hannah were holding on to.
reflections.q: “Only let the LORD establish His word.”

reflections.title: Nurturing the Life of the Spirit
reflections.html: In union with Christ, we are called to nurture the life of the Spirit until it reaches maturity, depending entirely on God to confirm His work in us.
reflections.q: In union with Christ, we are called to nurture the life of the Spirit until it reaches maturity, depending entirely on God to confirm His work in us.

24.brief: When Samuel is weaned, Hannah brings him to the house of the LORD in Shiloh with three bulls, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine. The narrator’s note that the child was young underscores the cost of what she is giving.
24.explain:
“Now when she had weaned him, she took him up with her,”

When the time came, Hannah kept her vow. She “took him up with her” to Shiloh.

“with three bulls, one ephah of flour, and a skin of wine,”

She brought generous offerings: “three bulls, one ephah of flour, and a skin of wine.” An “ephah” was a substantial dry measure of grain. Flour and wine accompanied animal sacrifices as grain and drink offerings (Numbers 15:8–10). The offerings expressed thanksgiving and the fulfillment of her vow. She came to Shiloh not with a token but with an offering that matched the weight of what God had done.

“and brought him to the house of the LORD in Shiloh.”

She brought Samuel “to the house of the LORD in Shiloh,” the place where she had prayed years before.

“And the child was young.”

The narrator adds, “the child was young.” The Hebrew is literally ‘the boy was a boy,’ emphasizing how small he was. The note underscores the cost of what Hannah was giving. She was leaving a little child at the sanctuary, in the care of an old priest whose own sons were corrupt.
24.notes:
The Hebrew text reads “three bulls.” The Septuagint, a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel, and the ancient Syriac translation read ‘a three-year-old bull.’ The traditional Hebrew reading probably arose when a scribe divided two Hebrew words at the wrong place.

Verse 25 mentions “a bull,” which some see as support for the single three-year-old bull; others note that one of three bulls could be singled out as the main sacrifice.

An ephah was a dry measure. Estimates of its modern equivalent vary.

reflections.title: The Costly Joy of Fulfillment
reflections.html: When Hannah finally brought Samuel to Shiloh, she did not come empty-handed. She brought a three-year-old bull (or three bulls, depending on the textual tradition), an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine. It was a lavish offering, a significant financial sacrifice far beyond what was required. She did not bring her child grudgingly but with a celebration, honoring the loss of her son to the Lord’s service. True gratitude for answered prayer produces extravagant, costly worship. When you give your most precious gift to God, give it with overflowing generosity, not reluctance.
reflections.q: When Hannah finally brought Samuel to Shiloh, she did not come empty-handed.

reflections.title: Blood, Bread, and Wine
reflections.html: The surrender of the child was framed by blood, bread, and wine: the bull, the flour, and the wine. True consecration to God is never cheap. Whatever we offer to God must come by way of the shed blood and with the joy of the Spirit. The scene gives a vivid foreshadowing of the Lord’s Table and Christ’s ultimate sacrifice. We bring our lives to the Father, fully accepted only through the sacrifice of the true Offering, Christ, and the wine of the New Covenant.
reflections.q: The surrender of the child was framed by blood, bread, and wine: the bull, the flour, and the wine.

reflections.title: A Feast Where She Used to Starve
reflections.html: Bull, flour, and wine were the makings of a thanksgiving feast. The barren, weeping woman of verse 7, who would not eat at Shiloh, was now bringing a feast to the very place where she used to starve.
reflections.q: Bull, flour, and wine were the makings of a thanksgiving feast.

reflections.title: Minimum or Outpouring?
reflections.html: Are our offerings to God minimum requirements, or lavish outpourings of gratitude?
reflections.q: Are our offerings to God minimum requirements, or lavish outpourings of gratitude?

25.brief: They slaughter a bull and bring the child to Eli. Sacrifice and the presentation of Samuel stand side by side, so that handing over her son takes place as an act of worship.
25.explain:
“Then they slaughtered a bull,”

The family offered the sacrifice. “A bull” was slaughtered, probably as a burnt offering or a vow offering in fulfillment of Hannah's promise.

“and brought the child to Eli.”

Then they brought “the child to Eli.” Sacrifice and the presentation of Samuel stand side by side, so that handing over her son took place as an act of worship. Hannah was not abandoning her child; she was offering him to the LORD in the place where she had prayed for him. Eli, who had once misjudged her, now received the answer to the prayer he had blessed.

reflections.title: The Blood Before the Living Sacrifice
reflections.html: “Then they slaughtered a bull, and brought the child to Eli.” Before Samuel was handed over for ministry, blood was shed. The blood of the substitute cleared the way for the living sacrifice to be presented. This points to the order fulfilled in Christ: we do not offer ourselves to God to make ourselves acceptable. We belong to Him and offer ourselves because Jesus has first given Himself for us. His blood opens the way for us to become living sacrifices (Romans 12:1–2). The cross is not the reward for our consecration; it is the ground on which we belong to Him.
reflections.q: “Then they slaughtered a bull, and brought the child to Eli.”

reflections.title: The Altar Before the Dedication
reflections.html: The sacrifice comes before the presentation of the child. No one is dedicated to the Lord’s service without first passing by way of the altar and the blood. No life is truly given to God apart from the altar of sacrifice. Consecration rests on a substitutionary sacrifice; the blood and the calling cannot be separated.
reflections.q: The sacrifice comes before the presentation of the child.

reflections.title: Death Works So Life Can Work
reflections.html: The dead sacrifice and the living child stand side by side: the blood was shed so the boy could serve. The cross must come before the ministry. Death works in us so that life can work in others (2 Corinthians 4:12).
reflections.q: The dead sacrifice and the living child stand side by side: the blood was shed so the boy could serve.

reflections.title: A Short Sentence Holding a Mother’s Heart
reflections.html: The brevity of the sentence is striking. A heart-wrenching moment, a mother handing her small child to a priest, is told in a few words, anchored entirely by the slaughter of the sacrifice.
reflections.q: The brevity of the sentence is striking.

reflections.title: Surrender Must Become Action
reflections.html: It is one thing to tell God that something belongs to Him while the moment of giving still lies ahead; it is another to follow through once what we are surrendering has become precious to us. True surrender remains surrender when we actually let go.
reflections.q: It is one thing to tell God that something belongs to Him while the moment of giving still lies ahead; it is another to follow through once what we are surrendering has become precious to us.

26.brief: Hannah addresses Eli with a respectful oath and reminds him that she is the woman who stood beside him there, praying to the LORD. She connects this moment directly to the prayer he once misjudged.
26.explain:
“And she said, ‘O my lord! As your soul lives, my lord,’”

Hannah addressed Eli respectfully. “O my lord” was a polite form of address, and “As your soul lives” was a solemn affirmation, like saying ‘as surely as you live’ (compare 17:55). She was about to make a statement she wanted Eli to take seriously.

“I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the LORD.”

She reminded Eli who she was. “I am the woman who stood by you here.” Years earlier, Eli had watched her mouth and thought she was drunk (1:12–14). Now she connected this moment directly to that prayer. The woman Eli had rebuked was standing before him again, this time with the answer in her arms.
26.notes: The phrase “stood by you here” indicates that Hannah prayed standing, a common posture for prayer in Israel. The detail also places her near Eli's seat by the doorpost (1:9).

reflections.title: The Secret Place Revealed
reflections.html: Hannah introduced herself not by her family line but by her posture of prayer: “I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the LORD.” She pointed Eli back to her moment of desperate, silent prayer. The results of secret prayer are eventually seen in public. The prayer that was hidden in her heart, and misunderstood by the priest, was now vindicated by the child at her side.
reflections.q: Hannah introduced herself not by her family line but by her posture of prayer: “I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the LORD.”

reflections.title: Back to the Place of Weeping
reflections.html: Hannah reminded Eli where she had once stood. She claimed the geography of her former agony as the site of her present victory. God can turn places of painful prayer into places of testimony. Bring your answered prayers back to the very place where you once wept.
reflections.q: Hannah reminded Eli where she had once stood.

reflections.title: Sorrow Does Not Have the Final Word
reflections.html: Hannah stood again where she had once wept, but now Samuel stood beside her as the living answer to that very prayer. This finds its fullest expression in Jesus. The cross, the place of deepest sorrow, became through His resurrection the great testimony of God’s saving victory. In Christ, sorrow does not have the final word.
reflections.q: Hannah stood again where she had once wept, but now Samuel stood beside her as the living answer to that very prayer.

reflections.title: Known as One Who Prayed
reflections.html: The most glorious identity a person can carry is “the one who stood here praying.” Our truest identity in the kingdom of God is forged in our secret history of intercession. God transformed Hannah’s identity from her affliction, the barren woman, to her victory, the praying woman. In Christ our past shame is erased, and we are known by our communion with the Father. Let your defining characteristic be that you are a person of prayer. If you came back to this altar years from now, could you say, “I am the one who stood here praying”?

reflections.title: Prayer Changed Her Presence
reflections.html: Eli likely did not recognize her. Her face was different, she was no longer fasting, and she was holding a small child. Prayer had changed even her physical presence.
reflections.q: Eli likely did not recognize her.

27.brief: Hannah testifies, “For this child I prayed,” and declares that the LORD has granted the petition she asked of Him. She gives the LORD full credit for Samuel’s birth.
27.explain:
“For this child I prayed,”

Hannah testified to what God had done. “For this child I prayed.” The words point to the boy beside her. He was the answer to the prayer Eli had seen.

“and the LORD has granted me my petition which I asked of Him.”

She declared that “the LORD has granted” her petition. She gave the LORD full credit for Samuel's birth. The word “petition” and the verb “asked” repeat the language of Eli's blessing (1:17). Eli had prayed that the God of Israel would grant her petition; now Hannah announced that He had. God had heard both the prayer and the blessing, and He had answered.
27.notes: In Hebrew, the verb sha'al, ‘to ask,’ and its related noun appear twice in this verse, behind “my petition” and “I asked.” They appear twice more in the next verse, behind “I also have lent him” and “he shall be lent.”

reflections.title: Radical Acknowledgment of the Source
reflections.html: “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition.” Hannah’s testimony was simple. She took no credit for her fruitfulness. She did not boast to Peninnah; she pointed entirely to the LORD, who heard and answered. The life she held was a direct gift from heaven. Testify boldly to what God has done, and connect the answered prayer directly to the God who gave it.
reflections.q: “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition.”

reflections.title: The Invisible Petition Made Visible
reflections.html: Hannah held up the boy as the tangible answer to invisible groans. The prayer no one could hear had become a child everyone could see. Samuel was, in a sense, the word made flesh in her own life: a spiritual petition that took on physical form. Answered prayer is the visible fruit of the hidden union between the believer’s asking and God’s giving.
reflections.q: Hannah held up the boy as the tangible answer to invisible groans.

reflections.title: Confirming Eli’s Blessing
reflections.html: Hannah used the same language Eli had used in verse 17, “grant your petition.” She was confirming to the priest that his blessing had come true.
reflections.q: Hannah used the same language Eli had used in verse 17, “grant your petition.”

reflections.title: Pray Specifically
reflections.html: Specific prayer can become unmistakable testimony. Hannah could say, “For this child I prayed,” and stand before Eli with the very answer beside her. There is value in bringing our desires before God specifically, so that we can recognize His answer when it comes.
reflections.q: Specific prayer can become unmistakable testimony.

reflections.title: Tell the One Who Saw Your Sorrow
reflections.html: Hannah deliberately returned to name what God had done rather than let it pass uncredited. There is life in telling plainly, to someone who once saw our sorrow, exactly what the Lord has done.
reflections.q: Hannah deliberately returned to name what God had done rather than let it pass uncredited.

reflections.title: Yes and Amen in Him
reflections.html: Christ Himself is the ultimate answer to all the groaning of humanity; in Him all the promises of God are “Yes” and “Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
reflections.q: Christ Himself is the ultimate answer to all the groaning of humanity; in Him all the promises of God are “Yes” and “Amen” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

reflections.title: For This I Prayed, and This God Did
reflections.html: God is a prayer-answering God who delights to grant the petitions of His people. Our testimony can be just this simple: “For this I prayed, and this God did.”
reflections.q: God is a prayer-answering God who delights to grant the petitions of His people.

28.brief: Hannah declares that she has lent Samuel to the LORD for as long as he lives, fulfilling her vow, and they worship the LORD there. The child received through asking is now given back to the LORD for life.
28.explain:
“Therefore I also have lent him to the LORD;”

Hannah fulfilled her vow. “I also have lent him to the LORD.” “Lent” comes from the same root as ‘ask.’ The sense is that what she asked from the LORD, she now gives over to the LORD. The English word “lent” should not be taken to mean that she expected to get him back. She was giving him for life.

“as long as he lives he shall be lent to the LORD.”

The dedication was permanent: “as long as he lives.” The child received through asking was now given back to the LORD for life. Hannah kept the vow she had made in bitterness of soul, and she kept it in joy.

“So they worshiped the LORD there.”

The chapter ends with worship. “They worshiped the LORD there.” The place of Hannah's tears had become the place of her thanksgiving. Her song in the next chapter (2:1–10) is her response to this dedication.
28.notes:
“I also have lent him” translates a form of the Hebrew verb sha'al that means to grant or hand over what was asked for. Having asked the LORD for a son, Hannah now gives that son back to Him. “He shall be lent” translates sha'ul, the form meaning ‘asked for,’ which is spelled exactly like the name Saul.

Some scholars have argued from this wordplay that the birth account was originally told about Saul. Others have judged the wordplay too slight a basis for that theory, and the account as it stands tells of Samuel.

The Hebrew text reads literally ‘he worshiped.’ The subject is not named; it most likely refers to Elkanah, though Samuel or Eli are also possible.

The ancient Syriac translation reads the plural, ‘they worshiped,’ as the NKJV does. The Septuagint and a Hebrew manuscript of Samuel from Qumran point to a reading in which Hannah left Samuel there and worshiped, and one Septuagint manuscript lacks the clause altogether.

reflections.title: The Irrevocable Yield
reflections.html: “Therefore I also have lent him to the LORD.” The word for “lent” or “dedicated” comes from the same root as “asked” (sha’al), the word Hannah tied to Samuel’s name. She asked for him, and now she gives him back. What we receive through prayer must be yielded back to the Giver. If we clutch the blessing, it becomes an idol; if we dedicate it to God, it becomes a kingdom legacy.
reflections.q: “Therefore I also have lent him to the LORD.”

reflections.title: The Eternal Loan
reflections.html: “As long as he lives he shall be lent to the LORD.” Hannah returned what she had asked for. This reveals the mystery of stewardship: we only truly keep what we completely give up to God. And in response to that total surrender, the verse ends in worship. The ultimate goal of every answered prayer is worship.
reflections.q: “As long as he lives he shall be lent to the LORD.”

reflections.title: Loving the Giver More Than the Gift
reflections.html: Faith does not clutch the answer once it comes. Hannah had desperately sought Samuel, but when God gave him to her, she gave him back. Her surrender showed that she loved the Giver more than the gift she had so deeply desired. It is the same pattern the Father would one day complete in reverse: He so loved the world that He gave His only Son (John 3:16), so that everything we now receive from Him, including our very lives, might be freely given back.
reflections.q: Faith does not clutch the answer once it comes.

reflections.title: Holding the Gift Without It Holding Us
reflections.html: Like Abraham with Isaac, Hannah shows the pattern: God gives the gift, we offer it back, and then we can hold the gift without the gift holding us.
reflections.q: Like Abraham with Isaac, Hannah shows the pattern: God gives the gift, we offer it back, and then we can hold the gift without the gift holding us.

reflections.title: She Gave Up a Boy and Gained a Prophet
reflections.html: Having finally received the desire of her heart, Hannah gave it back permanently. She gave up the boy, but she gained a prophet. By surrendering her motherly possession of him, she released him to become a deliverer for the nation.
reflections.q: Having finally received the desire of her heart, Hannah gave it back permanently.

reflections.title: Never Wasted in His Hands
reflections.html: What is placed wholly in God’s hands is never wasted. Samuel was never Hannah’s to keep in the first place; surrendered fully to God, his life became far more than she could ever have made it by holding on.
reflections.q: What is placed wholly in God’s hands is never wasted.

reflections.title: We Are Not Our Own
reflections.html: Total consecration is the fitting response to divine grace. Just as Hannah lent Samuel to the LORD for a lifetime, we yield our lives entirely to Christ, for we are not our own; we were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
reflections.q: Total consecration is the fitting response to divine grace.

reflections.title: Who Worshiped There?
reflections.html: “And he worshiped the LORD there.” The final worshiper is most likely Elkanah, or possibly the young Samuel himself. Either way, the chapter that began in rivalry and tears ends in worship at Shiloh.
reflections.q: “And he worshiped the LORD there.”

reflections.title: What Is Your Samuel?
reflections.html: What is your “Samuel,” and have you dedicated it back to the Lord?
reflections.q: and have you dedicated it back to the Lord?
